A test is a function such as `func TestParse(t *testing.T)` in a file ending `_test.go`. It can use the production package name, or a package name ending `_test` to exercise the exported API from outside the package.

A table-driven test keeps cases in data and the assertion in code. `t.Run` gives each case a separate name in the result stream. No external test framework is required.

guide.caption: Production code and test code are compiled together according to the chosen test package.
guide.practical: Write tables around the observable contract: normal input, boundaries and failures. Use Fatal when continuing would make the rest of the test meaningless, and Error when collecting several independent mismatches is useful. Keep test data independent so adding a case does not change another case’s state.
guide.title: A test is ordinary Go with a testing entry point
guide.watchOut: Tests in package name_test exercise the exported API; tests in the same package can also inspect unexported details.

lessons.objective: Write a table-driven test and run it locally.
lessons.title: Tests are a file, not a framework

lessons.explanation:
A package's name becomes the qualifier callers read: `http.Server` is clearer than `http.HTTPServer`. Prefer short, descriptive lowercase names. Singular names are common, but useful standard-library packages such as `strings`, `errors` and `slices` are plural.

Avoid needless repetition between package and exported name. `chart.New` can be clear for a package centered on one chart type; a package with several constructors may need more specific names. Read the whole selector to judge it.

guide.caption: Read exported names with their package qualifier before deciding whether they are clear.

nodes.detail: The two words are read together
nodes.label: Public name

guide.practical: Prefer short, specific package names that describe the responsibility. Avoid repeating the package name in every exported identifier: cache.Store is usually clearer than cache.CacheStore. An import alias resolves a local naming conflict without changing the package’s own public name.
guide.title: The package name becomes part of every selector
guide.watchOut: A vague package name such as utils tends to gather unrelated responsibilities and makes the dependency direction harder to understand.

lessons.objective: Name a package and its exported function without repeating yourself.
lessons.question: What does this print?
lessons.title: The package name is half the API

lessons.explanation:
A package initializes its variables using their dependency relationships, then runs its init functions in source order as presented to the compiler. Imported packages finish initialization before the importing package. `main` starts after the program's initialization completes.

Do not depend on arbitrary file presentation order for important behavior. Explicit constructors make configuration and recoverable failure handling visible. An init function takes no arguments and returns no result, though it can register a driver or format as a deliberate import side effect.

guide.caption: Within a package, variable dependency analysis also affects initialization order.
guide.practical: Prefer explicit constructors when configuration or failure handling belongs to the caller. Init functions take no arguments and return no result, which makes them a poor place for recoverable setup. Several init functions are allowed, but hidden dependence on file presentation order makes maintenance harder.
guide.title: Initialization follows dependencies before main
guide.watchOut: A goroutine started during init may continue running while later initialization proceeds. It needs explicit synchronization if ordering matters.

lessons.objective: Predict the order of package variables, init and main.
lessons.question: In what order do the lines appear?
lessons.title: init runs before main, and order is defined

lessons.explanation: A repository, a module and a package can be three different boundaries. Trace the module path plus the package subdirectory before changing imports. A version suffix is part of the import identity; a folder name alone does not decide which source the compiler builds.
lessons.objective: Resolve module roots, import paths, internal visibility and major-version suffixes.

cautions: A module versions a set of packages together. A package groups source in one directory; the repository name does not override its declared package identifier.
designGuide.cost: Each extra module adds versioning, publishing and consumer-compatibility work; package boundaries inside one module are cheaper.
strengths: Resolve module roots, import paths, internal visibility and major-version suffixes.

alternatives: Every source file is a separately versioned module
The repository name always determines the package identifier
quiz.correct: One release can contain many directory packages
quiz.explanation: A module versions a set of packages together. A package groups source in one directory; the repository name does not override its declared package identifier.
quiz.hint: Follow go.mod, then the subdirectory of the import.
quiz.question: How do a module and a package relate?

review.answer: One release can contain many directory packages

sections.body: Start from the working directory and inspect the active module and workspace. A nested go.mod starts another module and can make ./... skip source you expected to test. Package names need not match the final path element, although a clear correspondence usually makes code easier to read.
sections.code:
go env GOMOD GOWORK
go list -f '{{.ImportPath}} => {{.Dir}}' ./...
go list -m
sections.title: Locate the source that is actually selected
sections.walkthrough: GOMOD identifies the active module file. The package listing maps each import to a real directory, so an unexpected checkout or nested module becomes visible before you edit source.

sections.body: For ordinary module-aware releases at v2 and above, /v2 is part of the module and import path. Updating a version number without updating the path is not a compatible major upgrade. Some legacy modules use +incompatible; do not copy that exception into a new module design.
sections.code:
module example.com/catalog/v2

go 1.24.0
sections.title: Major versions have distinct identities
sections.walkthrough: The root package is imported as example.com/catalog/v2; a subpackage is example.com/catalog/v2/search. The file illustrates path structure rather than asking you to fetch a nonexistent example module.

sections.body: An internal directory limits which importers may reach a package; it is not an authorization boundary for running code. A package import cycle fails before the program starts. Move a small consumer-owned contract or shared value to an acyclic boundary instead of solving a cycle with init side effects.
sections.title: Keep ownership inside one dependency direction

reading.takeaway: Identify the active module and actual package directory first. Treat a new major import path as an API migration, and keep the dependency graph acyclic.

lessons.title: A module is a release boundary; a package is a directory

lessons.explanation: A direct require is not a lock on every transitive dependency. Other requirements can raise the selected version of the same module path. Diagnose the graph first, then test the change that actually enters the build; repeatedly deleting go.sum does not explain an upgrade.
lessons.objective: Read minimal version selection and investigate a transitive upgrade without guessing.

cautions: The selected version for one module path must satisfy the graph’s minimum requirements. go.sum records content hashes, not a request for the newest version.
designGuide.cost: A graph change can raise transitive versions; review and regression-test the selected delta instead of counting edited require lines.
strengths: Read minimal version selection and investigate a transitive upgrade without guessing.

alternatives: go.sum always requests the newest release
The package name selects a random matching version
quiz.correct: Other requirements can raise the selected minimum
quiz.explanation: The selected version for one module path must satisfy the graph’s minimum requirements. go.sum records content hashes, not a request for the newest version.
quiz.hint: Separate a requirement edge from the selected build list.
quiz.question: Why can a transitive module be newer than your direct requirement?

review.answer: Other requirements can raise the selected minimum

sections.body: go list -m all describes the selected module versions for this build. go mod graph shows requirement edges, while go mod why explains why a package or module is needed. These answer different questions; none proves that an upgraded API preserves your application behavior.
sections.code:
go list -m all
go mod graph
go mod why -m golang.org/x/text
go list -m -u all
sections.title: Observe the build list
sections.walkthrough: Compare the requirement edges with the selected build list. A higher minimum from another dependency can explain a version that is newer than the one your own require line originally mentioned.

sections.body: Choose a reviewed version rather than upgrading everything during an outage. go get changes the dependency graph; go install package@version installs a command separately. Inspect go.mod and go.sum together and run affected integration tests, including the error and timeout behavior of upgraded clients.
sections.code:
go get golang.org/x/text@v0.23.0
go mod tidy
git diff -- go.mod go.sum
go test ./...
sections.title: Change one dependency and review the result
sections.walkthrough: This is an example of a specific upgrade in a development checkout, not a recommendation that the illustrated version is current. Inspect the resulting graph and choose an appropriate supported version for your project.

sections.body: A replace can redirect source while leaving you unaware that CI builds something else. A retract signals a version that authors advise against; it does not erase an already selected dependency. Keep a minimal reproducer for an incompatible transitive update instead of treating a clean cache as a correctness test.
sections.title: Avoid false fixes

reading.takeaway: Inspect the selected graph, explain the edge that raised a version, and validate the smallest dependency change with the application behaviors it affects.

lessons.title: Explain the selected version before running go get

lessons.explanation: A download failure may come from version discovery, credentials, a proxy, the checksum database or local cache integrity. Treat those as separate layers. A checksum records content identity; it neither proves the code is safe nor decides which version the dependency graph chooses.
lessons.objective: Diagnose downloads without leaking private paths or disabling integrity checks globally.

cautions: A checksum verifies the expected content of a version. It does not select that version, certify its behavior or establish that no vulnerability is known.
designGuide.cost: Private fetches need reliable credentials and transport; retaining integrity checks makes failures easier to investigate.
strengths: Diagnose downloads without leaking private paths or disabling integrity checks globally.

alternatives: That the module has no vulnerabilities
That this module version is the newest available
quiz.correct: Records verified content; it does not select versions
quiz.explanation: A checksum verifies the expected content of a version. It does not select that version, certify its behavior or establish that no vulnerability is known.
quiz.hint: Integrity, authorization and dependency selection are different layers.
quiz.question: What does a go.sum entry establish?

review.answer: Records verified content; it does not select versions

sections.body: Read configuration before changing it. Private module patterns affect how the Go command consults public services; they do not log you in to a private repository. Use the environment and credential mechanisms approved for that repository, and keep tokens out of module URLs and command history.
sections.code:
go env GOPROXY GOPRIVATE GONOPROXY GONOSUMDB
go mod download -json
go mod verify
sections.title: Inspect effective settings
sections.walkthrough: The commands distinguish download provenance and local verification from compilation. Download JSON can contain private module paths, so inspect it locally and redact paths before sharing an incident report.

sections.body: GOPRIVATE is a pattern list for private module path prefixes. Configure a company-specific pattern in the environment of the developer shell and CI job. GOPROXY fallback with comma versus pipe has different failure behavior; choose deliberately instead of masking every proxy error with direct access.
sections.code:
# Example only: replace the organization path.
GOPRIVATE=github.com/example-company/* go mod download
sections.title: Scope private paths narrowly
sections.walkthrough: The assignment applies to this one command rather than silently altering every future shell. It still needs separately configured repository credentials and a network route to the source.

sections.body: A checksum mismatch deserves investigation of the module version, proxy and local files. Do not teach a build to accept changed content under an existing version. go.sum can include go.mod checksums for modules whose source is not used, and it may change after tidy without representing a new executable dependency.
sections.title: Keep integrity and availability separate

reading.takeaway: Trace discovery, transport, credentials and checksums independently. Narrow private patterns and preserve integrity verification for public dependencies.

lessons.title: Checksums, proxies and private modules solve different problems

lessons.explanation: A checkout can pass because go.work supplies a sibling module or replace points to a local directory that no consumer has. That success tests the local composition, not the published module. Keep a second path that exercises the version and files a real downstream user receives.
lessons.objective: Use go.work and replace for development while checking what an independent consumer builds.

cautions: GOWORK=off removes the local workspace composition. That exposes missing published requirements and APIs that only worked through sibling modules or local replacements.
designGuide.cost: Fast local iteration needs a separate isolated-consumer check to expose unpublished assumptions before release.
strengths: Use go.work and replace for development while checking what an independent consumer builds.

alternatives: It disables all tests that touch the filesystem
It automatically publishes every workspace module
quiz.correct: Can depend on unpublished local replacements
quiz.explanation: GOWORK=off removes the local workspace composition. That exposes missing published requirements and APIs that only worked through sibling modules or local replacements.
quiz.hint: Compare the local composition with a separate consumer.
quiz.question: Why also test with GOWORK=off?

review.answer: Can depend on unpublished local replacements

sections.body: Inspect the active workspace and replacements before comparing two machines. A local replacement changes source selection; a replace line in a dependency is not automatically inherited by its consumers. Avoid committing an absolute workstation path as a release dependency.
sections.code:
go env GOWORK
go work edit -json
go list -m -json all
sections.title: See the workspace and overrides
sections.walkthrough: The workspace JSON lists participating module directories; the module listing shows replacements used by the build. Compare these facts before assuming a compiler or operating-system bug.

sections.body: Run checks with GOWORK=off from the module directory and build a small independent consumer using the intended release version. A workspace root with several modules is not equivalent to one module where ./... automatically promises to cover every sibling.
sections.code:
GOWORK=off go mod tidy
GOWORK=off go test ./...
GOWORK=off go list -m all
sections.title: Verify the module on its own
sections.walkthrough: These commands deliberately ignore workspace composition. If the tests now fail, the difference is actionable: a missing requirement, an unpublished API or a dependency that only existed in the workspace.

sections.body: A coordinated local API change can make producer and consumer pass together while breaking older consumers. Release the producer compatibly, pin the consumer to the released version, then test that combination. Workspace convenience should not replace a compatibility matrix for separately released modules.
sections.title: Test migrations from both sides

reading.takeaway: Use local overrides to iterate quickly, then turn them off to test the module and its published consumer contract independently.

lessons.title: A local workspace can hide a broken release

lessons.explanation: A successful build in your checkout can depend on uncommitted generated files, platform-specific source or an asset missing from the release archive. Reproducibility concerns the whole input set: toolchain, selected modules, build constraints, generated files and embedded data.
lessons.objective: Check the source and assets that a clean build actually receives.

cautions: Compilation does not automatically invoke go generate. Generation is an explicit workflow step whose tool version and output need their own checks.
designGuide.cost: Vendor and generated assets increase repository and review volume; the payoff is explicit repeatable release inputs.
strengths: Check the source and assets that a clean build actually receives.

alternatives: Before every compile of a generated package
Only when the module cache is empty
quiz.correct: Runs only when explicitly requested
quiz.explanation: Compilation does not automatically invoke go generate. Generation is an explicit workflow step whose tool version and output need their own checks.
quiz.hint: Distinguish an explicit generation step from compilation.
quiz.question: When does go build automatically run go generate?

review.answer: Runs only when explicitly requested

sections.body: go list exposes which source and embedded files belong to the selected target. Build tags and GOOS/GOARCH can select different implementations. An import that works on your Mac may require cgo or assembly on another target; do not infer portability from a package download.
sections.code:
go list -f '{{.GoFiles}} {{.IgnoredGoFiles}} {{.EmbedFiles}}' ./...
go list -deps ./...
go env GOOS GOARCH CGO_ENABLED
sections.title: Inspect the selected files and dependencies
sections.walkthrough: The file selection is concrete evidence for the current build configuration. Repeat it for the intended target and inspect dependency code before promising portability to a restricted runtime.

sections.body: Regenerate vendor after reviewing a dependency change and check it with the corresponding go.mod. Vendor mode deliberately uses that tree instead of treating a full module cache as the source of truth. Toolchain and platform differences still matter.
sections.code:
go mod vendor
go test -mod=vendor ./...
go build -mod=vendor ./...
sections.title: Treat vendor as a derived dependency tree
sections.walkthrough: Run these in a development checkout or clean CI worktree. If module declarations and vendor metadata disagree, regenerate from the reviewed graph rather than hand-editing copied dependency source.

sections.body: go generate is explicit; go build does not run arbitrary generators for you. Check generated files or run a pinned generator in a defined build step. GopherForge currently does not preserve arbitrary non-Go embed assets while vendoring; learning native build commands here does not change that app limitation.
sections.title: Generated and embedded inputs are release inputs

reading.takeaway: Build the clean release input set, not just the current working tree. Verify tags, generated files and assets, and keep vendor consistent with the reviewed graph.

lessons.title: Reproduce the artifact: vendor, build tags and embedded files

lessons.explanation: A test can pass alone and fail when other packages or subtests run at the same time. Shared database names, environment variables, ports and mutable globals turn isolated test intent into interference. Give every test its own resources, and distinguish a data race from a wider coordination bug.
lessons.objective: Find races, test caching mistakes and shared integration fixtures before scaling concurrency.

cautions: Package test binaries and parallel subtests share downstream capacity. Isolate fixtures and bound their combined demand; the race detector does not size a database pool.
designGuide.cost: Isolation requires disposable fixtures and cleanup; parallelism still spends shared database and machine capacity.
strengths: Find races, test caching mistakes and shared integration fixtures before scaling concurrency.

alternatives: Increasing every pool to match the number of tests
Running with the race detector instead of managing resources
quiz.correct: Need isolated fixtures and a shared capacity budget
quiz.explanation: Package test binaries and parallel subtests share downstream capacity. Isolate fixtures and bound their combined demand; the race detector does not size a database pool.
quiz.hint: Count clients, test binaries and parallel subtests together.
quiz.question: What prevents tests from overloading one test database?

review.answer: Need isolated fixtures and a shared capacity budget

sections.body: -p controls how many packages are built or tested concurrently; -parallel controls parallel tests within one test binary; GOMAXPROCS affects Go execution parallelism. Setting all three high can overwhelm a shared database even though each individual test uses only a few connections.
sections.code:
go test -count=1 -shuffle=on ./...
go test -race -count=1 ./...
go test -p=2 -parallel=4 ./...
sections.title: Separate three kinds of parallelism
sections.walkthrough: A fresh run bypasses cached test results; shuffle exposes order dependence, and the race detector observes conflicting memory accesses on executed paths. None of these alone validates distributed database invariants.

sections.body: Use t.TempDir and t.Cleanup for filesystem state. Pick an OS-assigned listener port rather than a fixed global port. A test that mutates environment or process working directory must respect the testing package restrictions around parallel execution.
sections.title: Give temporary resources one owner
sections.walkthrough: The example is a test-file fragment importing testing and os. The test owns its directory and cleanup, and explicitly stays sequential because environment changes affect the whole process.

sections.body: Assert that work exits after cancellation and that database clients, rows, bodies and temporary servers are closed. A passing result with leaked goroutines can poison later tests or exhaust CI resources. Keep a failing shuffled seed or a deterministic reproducer rather than relying on repeated lucky retries.
sections.title: Test cancellation and resource release

reading.takeaway: Make test ownership explicit, bound package and subtest parallelism separately, and use race detection as evidence on exercised paths rather than a proof of correctness.

lessons.title: Parallel tests must own their mutable resources

lessons.explanation: An ns/op number describes one workload in one process. A production incident may instead come from pool wait, queue growth, a slow downstream service or allocation pressure. Start with the question you need to answer and preserve the workload and environment alongside the measurement.
lessons.objective: Measure allocations, concurrency and tail latency without mistaking closed-loop throughput for service capacity.

cautions: A microbenchmark measures its own loop and inputs. It may omit network, pool wait, queue growth and overload failures that dominate a real service.
designGuide.cost: Useful measurements require representative inputs, repeated runs and separate whole-service load evidence.
strengths: Measure allocations, concurrency and tail latency without mistaking closed-loop throughput for service capacity.

alternatives: That its p99 stays low at any request rate
That increasing goroutines will always increase throughput
quiz.correct: Does not establish whole-service capacity
quiz.explanation: A microbenchmark measures its own loop and inputs. It may omit network, pool wait, queue growth and overload failures that dominate a real service.
quiz.hint: Ask which delays and failures the benchmark does not include.
quiz.question: What can a low ns/op result prove about a database-backed API?

review.answer: Does not establish whole-service capacity

sections.body: Select one benchmark, include allocation reporting and repeat it. Keep setup outside the timed section where that matches the production operation. Optimizing a string conversion says little about the complete HTTP-to-database request unless the conversion dominates that request.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/codec -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkEncode -benchmem -count=5
go test ./internal/codec -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkEncode -cpu=1,2,4
sections.title: Repeat a focused microbenchmark
sections.walkthrough: Replace the package and benchmark with real ones. Repeated measurements expose noise; CPU variants reveal scaling effects, but they do not reproduce a network load generator or a remote database.

sections.body: RunParallel measures concurrent benchmark work using a closed loop. Retain observable work, avoid sharing an unsafe buffer, and define whether the benchmark measures hits, misses or both. Report failure rate, request sizes and queue limits for a service test instead of only a flattering average.
sections.title: Make parallel measurements honest
sections.walkthrough: This is a self-contained benchmark body importing testing. It intentionally includes the allocation and validates the result; use a representative payload before comparing implementations or drawing a capacity conclusion.

sections.body: At a steady incoming arrival rate, a saturated service can build a queue even while successful completions look fast. Observe p50/p95/p99 together with errors, active requests, pool checkout time and recovery after a burst. An unbounded queue delays failure instead of creating capacity.
sections.title: Look at the tail and overload response

reading.takeaway: Use benchmarks to answer narrow code questions, then test the complete service with an explicit arrival rate, bounded queues and tail-latency/error measurements.

lessons.title: A microbenchmark is not a capacity test

lessons.explanation: A high-latency request does not necessarily consume much CPU. It may be waiting on a mutex, scheduling, a network response or a connection pool. Capture evidence for the same workload and time window, and choose a profile that can explain the suspected delay.
lessons.objective: Use pprof and traces to investigate latency under load instead of increasing pools blindly.

cautions: A blocked request can spend most of its time waiting while consuming little CPU. Inspect queue, pool and synchronization delays as well as execution samples.
designGuide.cost: Profiles consume sampling overhead and need matching binaries, source revisions and a representative workload.
strengths: Use pprof and traces to investigate latency under load instead of increasing pools blindly.

alternatives: Every slow request must consume one full core
The garbage collector always accounts for all request latency
quiz.correct: May indicate waiting, not spare request capacity
quiz.explanation: A blocked request can spend most of its time waiting while consuming little CPU. Inspect queue, pool and synchronization delays as well as execution samples.
quiz.hint: Follow where requests spend time, including queues.
quiz.question: Why can a slow service have a mostly idle CPU?

review.answer: May indicate waiting, not spare request capacity

sections.body: CPU profiles show sampled execution time. Heap and allocation profiles answer different memory questions, so choose the sample type deliberately. Keep the test binary with its profiles and source revision; otherwise symbol names and comparisons can become misleading.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/codec -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkEncode -cpuprofile=cpu.out -memprofile=mem.out
go tool pprof -top cpu.out
go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_space -top mem.out
sections.title: Capture a bounded benchmark profile
sections.walkthrough: The commands create local profile artifacts and show where time or allocated bytes accumulate in the measured benchmark. They do not show every blocked request or replace pool wait metrics from a real service.

sections.body: Execution traces provide a timeline of goroutines and runtime activity. Block and mutex profiles need suitable runtime sampling configuration; collecting zero samples is not evidence that a service never waits. Profiling itself can affect the workload, so compare with the uninstrumented baseline.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/service -run TestBurst -trace=trace.out
go tool trace trace.out
go test ./internal/service -run TestBurst -blockprofile=block.out -mutexprofile=mutex.out
sections.title: Trace scheduling and explicit contention
sections.walkthrough: Replace TestBurst with a bounded representative test. Inspect overlap among waiting, CPU work and goroutine growth before changing concurrency or blaming the garbage collector.

sections.body: If pool checkout dominates, inspect request arrival rate and slow operations before raising pool limits. If allocation dominates, find retained objects and hot allocation sites. Expose production profiling only through an appropriately restricted diagnostic path because profiles can reveal application data and implementation details.
sections.title: Turn evidence into one falsifiable change

reading.takeaway: Match the profile to the suspected bottleneck and compare one controlled change. CPU time, allocated bytes and waiting time are related but different measurements.

lessons.title: Profile CPU, allocation and waiting as different bottlenecks

lessons.explanation: A burst of parallel compilation can exhaust memory before the program you are testing even starts. Build-cache misses, many packages, cgo and simultaneous jobs change the working set. Read the exact failing phase instead of assuming every slowdown is a goroutine scheduling issue in application code.
lessons.objective: Separate compiler work, runtime goroutines and caches when CI or a small machine stalls.

cautions: The -p build flag limits concurrent package work in the toolchain. It does not impose a request, goroutine or database-connection limit on the compiled application.
designGuide.cost: Lower package concurrency can increase build time while preventing memory exhaustion on a small worker.
strengths: Separate compiler work, runtime goroutines and caches when CI or a small machine stalls.

alternatives: The maximum number of HTTP requests in the built app
The database connection pool inside every package
quiz.correct: Bounds concurrent package work, not request goroutines
quiz.explanation: The -p build flag limits concurrent package work in the toolchain. It does not impose a request, goroutine or database-connection limit on the compiled application.
quiz.hint: The build process and the deployed service have separate budgets.
quiz.question: What does lowering go build -p primarily control?

review.answer: Bounds concurrent package work, not request goroutines

sections.body: GOCACHE stores build artifacts while GOMODCACHE stores downloaded modules; these are different resources. A cache hit is useful only when the input and target match. Clearing both as the first troubleshooting step can amplify an outage by forcing every job to fetch and compile again.
sections.code:
go env GOCACHE GOMODCACHE
go build -x -p=2 ./...
go test -p=2 ./...
sections.title: Observe rather than clear every cache
sections.walkthrough: The -x output reveals invoked tools and selected work. -p bounds build/test package parallelism, making it useful on constrained CI workers; it is separate from the deployed application’s connection and goroutine limits.

sections.body: Record the toolchain, module graph, target and build flags with the binary. go version -m inspects embedded build information. Repeat a clean dependency preparation in a fresh worktree or CI job when reproducibility is the question, instead of removing shared caches that other builds are using.
sections.code:
go version
go env GOOS GOARCH CGO_ENABLED
go build -trimpath -o ./bin/app ./cmd/app
go version -m ./bin/app
sections.title: Identify the runtime and the artifact
sections.walkthrough: The example assumes a real cmd/app package in your checkout. -trimpath removes certain local path information; it is not a substitute for pinning inputs or proving that two independently built artifacts have identical bytes.

sections.body: A container memory limit, runtime GOMEMLIMIT, compiler package parallelism and application concurrency solve different problems. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft runtime target and does not cap all process or kernel memory. Change the limit indicated by evidence; increasing all limits can move the failure to the host.
sections.title: Set budgets at the correct layer

reading.takeaway: Locate the failing phase and its resource owner. Bound build jobs separately from runtime work, and retain caches and build provenance deliberately.

lessons.title: Build concurrency also has a memory budget

lessons.explanation: The binary that formats, generates or analyzes your project is part of the workflow’s input. An unpinned command on PATH can silently change generated output or lint results. Keep the intended tool version and compiler selection explicit without confusing them with the libraries your application imports.
lessons.objective: Distinguish application dependencies, development commands and toolchain selection.

cautions: A reviewed tool pin makes CI’s command input reproducible. It still needs maintenance; it neither fixes all dependencies to one version nor removes future security work.
designGuide.cost: Pinned tools and compilers make output reproducible but add an explicit dependency-update responsibility.
strengths: Distinguish application dependencies, development commands and toolchain selection.

alternatives: To make every future security update unnecessary
To force all application libraries to the same version number
quiz.correct: Makes a command version explicit, not permanently safe
quiz.explanation: A reviewed tool pin makes CI’s command input reproducible. It still needs maintenance; it neither fixes all dependencies to one version nor removes future security work.
quiz.hint: Reproducibility and ongoing maintenance both matter.
quiz.question: Why pin development commands used by CI?

review.answer: Makes a command version explicit, not permanently safe

sections.body: The go directive states a module’s minimum Go version; a toolchain directive can suggest a toolchain for work on the main module. Depending on GOTOOLCHAIN, the go command may select or download another toolchain. CI should record its effective version instead of assuming PATH alone settles it.
sections.code:
go version
go env GOTOOLCHAIN GOMOD GOWORK
go mod edit -json
sections.title: Read both go and toolchain directives
sections.walkthrough: Inspect the active module and its directives together. In a restricted or offline environment, automatic toolchain downloads may not be available; prepare the required supported compiler before the build.

sections.body: A versioned go install command builds the selected command independently of the current module’s application dependencies. Newer Go versions also support tracking tools in go.mod; use the mechanism supported by your project toolchain and keep CI invocation consistent.
sections.code:
go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@v1.1.4
# Run the installed command from the configured GOBIN/PATH.
govulncheck ./...
sections.title: Install one reviewed command version
sections.walkthrough: The version is an illustrative pin, not a claim that it is the latest release. Review and update tool pins deliberately; pinning avoids surprise changes but does not make an old tool permanently appropriate.

sections.body: Document which generated outputs belong in version control and which are produced during a clean build. Test the generated delta and avoid a generator that relies on an uncommitted local replacement. Tool updates deserve a separate diff so semantic application changes remain reviewable.
sections.title: Generators need the same discipline

reading.takeaway: Record the effective compiler and reviewed tool versions. Keep generation reproducible and separate from ordinary library-version selection.

lessons.title: Pin the compiler and the tools that generate your code

lessons.explanation: Normal tests often cover the examples you already understand. Parsers and protocol boundaries also receive truncated, oversized and surprising inputs. Fuzzing explores input behavior, while vulnerability analysis asks whether known vulnerable code is reachable; the two tools answer different questions.
lessons.objective: Combine fuzzing, regression seeds and govulncheck without treating one green tool as complete assurance.

cautions: A weak property can pass even when the parser is wrong; choose an oracle tied to the contract.
designGuide.cost: Fuzzing spends a bounded compute budget; vulnerability findings require a maintained database and a reachable-code interpretation.
strengths: Combine fuzzing, regression seeds and govulncheck without treating one green tool as complete assurance.

alternatives: All possible inputs have been exhaustively checked
Dependency security no longer needs maintenance
quiz.correct: Report bounded evidence, not absence of every bug
quiz.explanation: A weak property can pass even when the parser is wrong; choose an oracle tied to the contract.
quiz.hint: State the input budget and the property actually asserted.
quiz.question: What does a passing bounded fuzz run establish?

review.answer: Report bounded evidence, not absence of every bug

sections.body: A useful fuzz property can check round trips, bounded output, valid parsing or equivalent behavior between implementations. Avoid a property that merely repeats the implementation. Bound input size and work so one accidental huge allocation does not consume the entire test budget.
sections.title: Choose a property with a real oracle
sections.walkthrough: The fragment imports testing and strconv and asserts a defined parse/format/parse round trip for accepted integers. Rejected strings are allowed by the parser contract. For your own parser, choose an equally explicit invariant and retain meaningful failures as regression seeds.

sections.body: Run a bounded fuzz campaign in a development environment and commit the small failing seed that explains a fixed bug. Ordinary go test reruns seed corpus inputs without launching an open-ended fuzz search. Vulnerability checks should use a reviewed current database and tool in connected CI.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/parser -fuzz=FuzzIntegerRoundTrip -fuzztime=20s
go test ./...
govulncheck ./...
sections.title: Give exploration and regression separate jobs
sections.walkthrough: The package path is illustrative and must contain the target. Fuzz time bounds the campaign; source-level vulnerability findings still need interpretation against the built artifact, call path and deployment configuration.

sections.body: A green scan only reports what the analyzer and its current vulnerability database know. It does not inspect every operational configuration or prove the absence of new vulnerabilities. A clean fuzz run means the explored inputs did not violate the asserted properties within that budget.
sections.title: Keep the conclusion proportional to the evidence

reading.takeaway: Use a meaningful bounded input property, retain regression seeds and analyze dependency findings in context. No single tool replaces behavior and deployment review.

lessons.title: Test unknown inputs and check reachable vulnerabilities

lessons.explanation: Imported packages initialize before main, and hidden setup can turn an import into a database connection, network wait or process-wide configuration decision. Make those dependencies visible at the composition root so startup, tests, retries and shutdown share a clear owner.
lessons.objective: Move fallible setup to an explicit owner and close shared resources after work drains.

cautions: The application component owns a shared client across requests, stops new work and drains existing work before closing it. Per-request pools multiply connection and startup costs.
designGuide.cost: Explicit startup and drain ordering take code, but make connection ownership, failure and tests observable.
strengths: Move fallible setup to an explicit owner and close shared resources after work drains.

alternatives: Each handler creates and forgets its own pool
Every imported package silently creates one in init
quiz.correct: Construct once; close after owned work drains
quiz.explanation: The application component owns a shared client across requests, stops new work and drains existing work before closing it. Per-request pools multiply connection and startup costs.
quiz.hint: Match resource lifetime to the component that uses it.
quiz.question: Who should own a service-wide database client?

review.answer: Construct once; close after owned work drains

sections.body: A constructor can return an error and accept a caller-owned context; init cannot return an error to its caller. Build shared clients once, check readiness with a bounded operation, and inject them into handlers. Do not construct a new pool every time a request arrives.
sections.title: Keep fallible startup explicit
sections.walkthrough: This is an application-structure fragment: loadConfig, openStore and serve belong to the application. The ordering exposes error propagation and ownership, while real shutdown must let active handlers finish before the shared store closes.

sections.body: Look for init functions, package-level constructors, mutable registries and side-effect imports. Some registration is intentional; expensive or fallible runtime work needs a visible reason. An import cycle is a package-graph problem, not a request concurrency problem.
sections.code:
go list -deps ./cmd/app
go list -f '{{.ImportPath}}: {{.Imports}}' ./internal/...
go test -count=1 ./...
sections.title: Audit hidden work in dependencies
sections.walkthrough: The commands show dependency paths and exercise a fresh test run. They do not inspect hidden effects automatically; combine the graph with reading constructors and initialization code at the boundaries you own.

sections.body: A readiness check should answer whether this instance can serve useful work, not hammer every dependency on every health probe. Stop new work, drain in-flight requests within a deadline, then close shared clients. Use a new bounded cleanup context when the request context is already canceled.
sections.title: Budget readiness and shutdown

reading.takeaway: Give fallible setup, request work and cleanup explicit owners. Reuse shared clients, preserve deadlines and test startup failure and shutdown ordering.

lessons.title: Package initialization is not a request-time connection factory

summary: Import paths, go.mod, go test and go vet, without a search engine.
title: Packages, modules and tooling
translationNote: Go's survey found professionals repeatedly returning to documentation for core go subcommands. That is not a knowledge gap so much as a model gap: once the module, the import path and the package directory line up in your head, the commands stop needing to be memorised.

lessons.explanation:
A send on an unbuffered channel does not complete until a receiver takes the value, and a receive does not complete until a sender provides one. It is a rendezvous, not a mailbox.

This is why the classic first Go deadlock is one line long: send on an unbuffered channel from the only goroutine there is, and nobody can ever arrive to meet it. The runtime notices that every goroutine is asleep and stops the program, which is a much better failure than a silent hang.

guide.caption: Completion of the exchange establishes synchronization between the participating goroutines.
guide.practical: Use an unbuffered channel when handing over a value should wait until a receiver is ready. Reason about both sides before launching work: a send performed before any receiver can run has nowhere to go. A channel communicates values and coordinates timing at the same time.
guide.title: A send and a receive meet at one point
guide.watchOut: Sending and then receiving on the same unbuffered channel in one goroutine blocks at the send.

lessons.objective: Say what blocks, and for how long, on a channel with no buffer.
lessons.question: What happens, and would a buffer of one change it?
lessons.title: An unbuffered channel is a meeting

lessons.explanation:
go f() starts f and immediately continues. There is no future to await and no value to collect, so the result has to come back through a channel or a shared variable protected by something.

The second half matters just as much: when main returns, the program exits and every remaining goroutine simply stops. A goroutine still blocked at that moment did not fail — it was never finished.

guide.caption: A go statement does not provide an implicit join or keep main alive.

nodes.detail: Begins a goroutine; returns no handle
nodes.label: Start

guide.practical: Pick a completion contract before starting a goroutine. A closed channel can signal one operation’s completion; a WaitGroup can join several operations. Pass cancellation and result paths deliberately so a caller can stop and collect the work it starts.
guide.title: Starting work is separate from waiting for it
guide.watchOut: When main returns, the program exits even if other goroutines have unfinished work.

lessons.objective: Get a result out of a goroutine, and know when the program stops waiting.
lessons.question: Is the second goroutine guaranteed to print?
lessons.source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	results := make(chan int)
	go func() { results <- 42 }()
	go func() { fmt.Println("this may never print") }()
	fmt.Println(<-results)
}
lessons.title: go returns nothing

lessons.explanation: Starting a goroutine creates an obligation: identify who asks it to stop and who observes that it has stopped. Canceling a context closes a signal; it does not terminate arbitrary Go code. Every blocking point must cooperate or have another bounded exit.
lessons.objective: Design a worker so it can stop waiting and its owner can wait for it to finish.

alternatives: Every goroutine using it has already exited
Every blocking primitive is forcibly interrupted
quiz.correct: Request a stop, then observe the worker finishing
quiz.explanation: A context only helps at code paths and APIs that observe it; cancellation alone does not join workers.
quiz.hint: Identify the stop signal and the acknowledgement as two separate events.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about cancellation and joining?

review.answer: Request a stop, then observe the worker finishing

sections.body: A producer may outlive its consumer. If the consumer returns early, an unconditional send can wait forever and keep its goroutine and reachable objects alive. Select between sending and cancellation.
sections.title: A blocked send needs an escape
sections.walkthrough: If the send and cancellation are both ready, select may choose either. Design the protocol to tolerate that race in intent; cancellation does not mean no operation can ever finish afterwards.

sections.body: A done channel acknowledges exit. The owner cancels, then waits. The worker must observe ctx, including inside downstream operations, or this wait can still block. Production shutdown also needs an overall timeout and a clear policy when a dependency refuses to return.
sections.title: Wait for the owned goroutine
sections.walkthrough: The worker closes done because it owns the completion signal. Do not close a work channel from an unrelated receiver while senders may still use it.

sections.body: For every worker, list start, inputs, outputs, stop signal and join point. Include error paths, not only success. Context does not interrupt a mutex lock or CPU loop automatically; choose primitives and loop checkpoints accordingly. A finalizer or the garbage collector is not a goroutine cleanup strategy.
sections.title: Use a lifecycle checklist

reading.takeaway: Cancellation communicates intent. A join or completion acknowledgement establishes that the owned work has actually stopped.

lessons.title: Cancellation is a request; joining proves exit

lessons.explanation:
Closing a channel says that no more values will be sent. Give that decision to the producer, or to a coordinator that knows all producers have finished. A receiver should not close a stream while senders may still use it.

Receivers can drain a closed buffered channel. `v, ok := <-ch` reports false only when the channel is closed and empty; `for v := range ch` then ends. Sending after close and closing twice both panic.

guide.caption: Close is a statement about the stream ending, not about discarding its queued values.
guide.practical: Give exactly one owner responsibility for closing. If multiple workers send, a coordinator can wait for all of them and close the results channel afterward. Receivers normally do not close because they cannot know that every sender has finished.
guide.title: The sender announces that no more values are coming
guide.watchOut: Sending to a closed channel or closing it twice panics. A channel used only for coordination does not always need to be closed.

lessons.objective: Decide who closes a channel, and why the other side must not.
lessons.title: The sender closes, the receiver ranges

lessons.explanation:
select blocks until one of its cases can proceed, and picks randomly among those that are ready. Adding a case for <-ctx.Done() turns any wait into a cancellable one.

The convention that makes this composable: context is the first parameter, it is passed rather than stored, and cancel is always deferred so the resources behind it are released on every path.

guide.caption: If several cases can proceed, select chooses one; source order is not a priority rule.
guide.practical: Make every potentially blocking send or receive part of the cancellation design. A context is a signal, so the operation must actually observe it. When a channel may close, use the receive boolean to distinguish the end of the stream from a real zero-valued item.
guide.title: Wait for work and cancellation together
guide.watchOut: Cancellation does not forcibly stop a goroutine. Work that never checks ctx.Done can keep running.

lessons.objective: Make a blocking operation cancellable without a flag or a kill switch.
lessons.title: select waits on several things; context says stop

lessons.explanation:
A channel is useful for transferring values and coordinating ownership. A mutex protects shared state that remains in place. Choose the mechanism that makes the invariant and its owner easiest to understand; neither mechanism is always faster.

Keep the mutex next to the data it protects and use the same locking rule for every read and write participating in the invariant. A small, clearly bounded critical section is easier to maintain than a lock whose protected state is scattered.

guide.caption: Every access participating in the shared invariant must follow the same locking rule.

nodes.detail: Read and modify the protected state
nodes.label: Update

nodes.detail: Allow the next owner to enter
nodes.label: Leave

guide.practical: Keep the critical section short and make lock ownership easy to see. A deferred unlock protects early returns, while an explicit unlock may be clearer around a small block. Use a channel when transferring ownership expresses the operation better than protecting shared mutable state.
guide.title: One lock protects one shared invariant
guide.watchOut: Protect reads as well as writes. Copying a used mutex or taking the same mutex twice can break the synchronization contract.

lessons.objective: Choose between a mutex and a channel for a given problem.
lessons.title: A mutex is for state; a channel is for handing over

lessons.explanation:
A fixed number of workers bounds concurrent processing. The producer sends jobs and closes the input stream after the last job. Workers consume it until it is drained. A coordinator waits for every worker before closing the output stream.

Results may need to be consumed while jobs are still being produced, or backpressure can deadlock the producer and workers. Add cancellation deliberately, and test termination as well as returned values.

guide.caption: A fixed worker count bounds concurrent processing, not the total number of jobs.

nodes.detail: Processes a job at a time
nodes.label: Worker A

guide.practical: Coordinate the full lifecycle: start workers, deliver jobs, close the jobs stream, wait for workers, then close the results stream. A separate results consumer may need to run while jobs are produced so backpressure cannot deadlock the producer.
guide.title: Bound the workers while letting jobs flow
guide.watchOut: Do not close results from an individual worker. Another worker may still be sending.

lessons.objective: Build a fixed set of workers that finishes cleanly.
lessons.title: The worker pool, written once

lessons.explanation: Concurrency is how work overlaps. Capacity is how much useful work the system can sustain. A thousand waiting goroutines do not give Redis a thousand extra cores or increase a database connection budget. They do consume memory, queue time and cancellation bookkeeping.
lessons.objective: Bound active workers and queued work according to the resource that actually limits throughput.

alternatives: It increases the dependency's physical capacity automatically
It removes all queueing and timeout costs
quiz.correct: Limits concurrent jobs, not requests per second
quiz.explanation: An unbounded population of goroutines waiting for a semaphore is still an unbounded queue.
quiz.hint: Find the slowest resource and the queue in front of it.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about a bounded worker pool?

review.answer: Limits concurrent jobs, not requests per second

sections.body: Suppose one downstream operation takes about 20 ms at the target load. Twenty concurrent operations can support roughly 1,000 operations per second in that simplified steady-state example. Real latency distributions, payload size and server limits change the result. Treat it as a sizing hypothesis, then measure tail latency and saturation.
sections.title: Start with a budget

sections.body: A fixed worker count bounds active calls. A bounded jobs channel also bounds queued work. A context-aware producer stops waiting when the request is no longer useful. This fragment shows the admission point; workers, cancellation and channel ownership must all belong to the same enclosing operation.
sections.title: Apply admission control before creating more work
sections.walkthrough: Do not launch a new goroutine for every rejected or blocked enqueue: that merely moves an unbounded queue from the channel into goroutine stacks.

sections.body: For request/response traffic, reject work that cannot meet its deadline or wait only within a bounded budget. For background work, use a durable queue if losing work is unacceptable. A worker pool limits concurrency, not requests per second; add rate limiting when the downstream contract is a rate. Track active calls, queue depth, queue age, errors and latency together.
sections.title: Pick a deliberate overload response

reading.takeaway: Bound workers, waiting work and waiting time. Size those limits from downstream behavior, then verify under load.

lessons.title: More goroutines are not more capacity

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Buffered Channels" page: `make(chan int, 100)` sends without a receiver until the buffer is full, and receives without a sender until it is empty. An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous. A buffered one is a mailbox of a known size.

The deadlock people then write is filling a buffer of 1 with two sends from the only goroutine there is. The buffer does not make the channel unbounded. It makes the bound visible in the `make`.

guide.caption: Buffering changes when a send blocks; it does not remove synchronization requirements.

nodes.detail: Two sends may queue without receivers
nodes.label: Space available

guide.practical: Choose capacity to express the intended amount of queued work. A small buffer can smooth bursts and decouple short timing differences. It cannot fix a missing receiver or an endless producer; once capacity is exhausted, backpressure still reaches the sender.
guide.title: A channel buffer has a finite number of slots
guide.watchOut: len(ch) is a momentary queue size, not a reliable precondition for a future send or receive.

lessons.objective: Send n values on a channel of capacity n without another goroutine.
lessons.title: A buffer is a mailbox, not a meeting

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Range and Close" page: `v, ok := <-ch` sets ok to false once the channel is closed and empty. `for v := range ch` is that loop written once. Only the sender closes. Sending after a close panics. Closing is not required for the garbage collector — only for telling a range there is nothing more.

Channels are not files. Most of them never close, because nobody is ranging. Close when a range (or an ok-receive) needs the signal.

guide.caption: A closed channel may still contain unread values.

nodes.detail: Ends after the buffer is empty
nodes.label: Drain and stop

guide.practical: Use range when the entire stream should be consumed until its producer finishes. If cancellation is also required, use a select loop and inspect the two-result receive. Assign close ownership to the producer or the coordinator that knows all producers are done.
guide.title: The receiver drains before the loop ends
guide.watchOut: Ranging over a nil channel blocks forever. A never-closed stream also never ends by itself.

lessons.objective: Drain a channel with range, and close it from the sender.
lessons.title: range over a channel ends when it closes

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Default Selection" page: a `default` case runs when no other case is ready, so the select returns instead of blocking. That is how you poll a channel, and how you try a send without parking the goroutine.

Without default, select waits. With it, "nothing ready" is a value you handle, not a hang. A busy loop of default-selects is a spin; use it for a single try, not as a substitute for a timer.

guide.caption: Default changes a blocking select into a try operation.

nodes.detail: Wait until a case can proceed
nodes.label: Blocking alternative

guide.practical: Use a default case when a skipped operation is part of the contract, such as a best-effort status update. A loop with default can spin continuously when no work is ready. Prefer a blocking select with cancellation or an explicit timing source for a waiting loop.
guide.title: Default means continue immediately when nothing is ready
guide.watchOut: Default does not run after a timeout and does not wait briefly. It is selected immediately when no communication is ready.

lessons.objective: Receive from a channel if a value is ready, and return if it is not.
lessons.title: default makes select try, not wait

lessons.explanation:
The Tour writes `ch <- v` and `v := <-ch` and then, in Effective Go, the type itself carries the arrow: `chan<- int` is send-only, `<-chan int` is receive-only. A function that only produces values should take `chan<- T`. The compiler then refuses a receive in that body, which is the whole point — the restriction is the API.

Conversion is one way: a bidirectional channel may be passed where a directional one is wanted. The other direction does not compile. Close is a send-side operation, so it belongs on `chan<- T`.

guide.caption: A bidirectional channel can be passed to a directional parameter.
guide.practical: Use direction in function signatures to communicate roles and let the compiler reject accidental reverse operations. The owner still needs a runtime lifecycle rule: a send-only parameter can close a channel, but that ability does not establish that it is the correct owner to do so.
guide.title: The type limits who may send or receive
guide.watchOut: Direction is a permission, not an ownership guarantee. Two senders can still race to close unless the design assigns one closer.

lessons.objective: Write a producer that takes chan<- int and closes it.
lessons.title: The arrow in the type is who may send

lessons.explanation:
Effective Go and the sync docs: `Once.Do(f)` runs f once, even when many goroutines call Do at the same time. After that, Do is a no-op. It is the right shape for a lazy setup that must not run twice — registering a driver, reading a config, seeding a generator.

Do not copy an Once after it has been used. Do not call Do with a different f and expect that second f to run. The once is on the Once, not on the function value.

guide.caption: Do does not return to any caller until the one initialization call has finished.

nodes.detail: The first caller runs the function
nodes.label: One shared Once

nodes.detail: Waits if initialization is in progress
nodes.label: Caller A

guide.practical: Keep the Once next to the state it protects, and keep that state in one shared object. It is suitable for initialization that must run at most once. Use another design if an operation may fail and needs retries; Once records the attempt rather than guaranteeing successful initialization.
guide.title: Concurrent callers share one completed initialization
guide.watchOut: If the function panics, Once still considers it done. Calling Do recursively on that same Once deadlocks.

lessons.objective: Initialise shared state without a lock you have to remember.
lessons.title: sync.Once runs a function one time, for everyone

lessons.explanation: A request owns more than the act of starting goroutines. It must know when its work has stopped and who retains the results. Go 1.25 added WaitGroup.Go, which combines task registration and launch. It reduces a common Add/launch ordering mistake without supplying cancellation, an error result or a concurrency budget.
lessons.objective: Use modern WaitGroup task ownership and explain its limits.

cautions: Use an error-aware group for returned task errors and keep a separate bounded cancellation path for work that may block.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: WaitGroup.Go joins tasks; it does not collect their errors
strengths: Use modern WaitGroup task ownership and explain its limits.
WaitGroup.Go registers owned work and Wait joins it. Cancellation, errors, panic policy and admission control remain separate parts of the design.

alternatives: Cancel the blocked send automatically
Collect and return its error
quiz.correct: Task registration and a join
quiz.explanation: Use an error-aware group for returned task errors and keep a separate bounded cancellation path for work that may block.
quiz.hint: Joining waits for exit; it cannot manufacture an exit path.
quiz.question: A WaitGroup task blocks forever on an uncancellable send. What does calling Wait do?

review.answer: Task registration and a join

sections.body: Each task writes to a distinct fixed result slot, and the owner reads results after Wait. That separates mutation by index without concurrently appending to a shared slice. Do not copy an already used WaitGroup or start an unrelated task after the owner has concluded that the group is empty.
sections.title: Register and join owned work
sections.walkthrough: This complete Go 1.25+ example relies on modern loop-declared variables, distinct output elements and an explicit join. It launches only three tasks. A production version with many inputs still needs admission control before launch, and result values must not share unsafe internal storage.

sections.body: The task function passed to WaitGroup.Go must not panic. It has no error return. Expected failures need an explicit result channel or an error-aware task group, and panic handling belongs to a deliberately chosen boundary. A WaitGroup cannot roll back side effects from a task that already ran.
sections.title: Do not infer an error protocol

sections.body: Wait does not take a context or kill a blocked task. A task doing I/O or sending a result must observe cancellation at each potentially blocking point. On shutdown, stop intake, signal cancellation where appropriate, wait for owned tasks and only then close the resources they use.
sections.title: Give cancellation its own path

sections.body: Use synchronization or a virtual-time test to hold a task at a known boundary. Verify the owner does not publish success until all required work finishes. A sleep followed by checking a counter depends on timing and may hide the same bug on a slower machine.
sections.title: Test completion rather than scheduling luck

reading.takeaway: WaitGroup.Go registers owned work and Wait joins it. Cancellation, errors, panic policy and admission control remain separate parts of the design.

lessons.title: WaitGroup.Go joins tasks; it does not collect their errors

lessons.explanation: Tests that sleep for a guessed interval are slow and sensitive to machine load. testing/synctest is a standard package in Go 1.25 and later. It runs a test bubble with virtual time and coordinated goroutine waiting. It is useful for in-process protocols, not a simulator for a remote database or every operating-system event.
lessons.objective: Use testing/synctest to assert a concurrent timeline deterministically.

cautions: Use the bubble for a deterministic in-process protocol and retain isolated integration tests for external services.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: Test time and cancellation without sleeping on the wall clock
strengths: Use testing/synctest to assert a concurrent timeline deterministically.
Describe the timeline and assert both early and final states. Virtual time makes supported concurrent tests reproducible; it does not replace real boundary integration checks.

alternatives: That real network failover was tested
That every goroutine schedule is safe
quiz.correct: Time inside a supported test bubble
quiz.explanation: Use the bubble for a deterministic in-process protocol and retain isolated integration tests for external services.
quiz.hint: Separate in-process evidence from an external system boundary.
quiz.question: A virtual-time unit test passes. What can it establish about a remote PostgreSQL failover?

review.answer: Time inside a supported test bubble

sections.body: Suppose work waits five seconds, publishes a result and exits. The test should establish that it has not published before the deadline and has completed after it. synctest.Wait lets in-bubble goroutines settle at supported blocking points so the assertions do not depend on the scheduler getting lucky.
sections.title: State the timeline first
sections.walkthrough: Save this complete example as timeline_test.go in a native Go 1.25+ module and run go test -race. The five-second sleep advances virtual time instead of imposing five seconds of wall-clock waiting. This lesson is a reading; it does not promise this diagnostic package on every WASI target.

sections.body: Model a worker waiting on either its timer or ctx.Done, then cancel at a known phase. Assert that the worker closes its completion signal and does not publish an unwanted result. Cancellation and a simultaneously ready result still need a documented policy; select is not a strict priority rule.
sections.title: Add a cancellation branch

sections.body: Virtual time advances when the package can establish the relevant in-bubble blocking state. External network servers, syscalls and objects outside the bubble have different constraints. Keep real integration tests for sockets and databases rather than treating a fast virtual-time test as evidence of remote behavior.
sections.title: Know the boundary of the bubble

sections.body: A deterministic test must still assert something meaningful. For a retry protocol, count durable effects and total attempts under a deadline; for cancellation, prove exit with a completion signal. A test that merely waits for the bubble to finish does not verify every business result.
sections.title: Keep the invariant after removing sleeps

reading.takeaway: Describe the timeline and assert both early and final states. Virtual time makes supported concurrent tests reproducible; it does not replace real boundary integration checks.

lessons.title: Test time and cancellation without sleeping on the wall clock

lessons.explanation: golang.org/x/sync/errgroup is a versioned external module, not part of sync. WithContext supplies a derived cancellation context and Wait returns a task error. Tasks must still cooperate with cancellation, and a limit on active tasks is different from a limit on queued input bytes or waiting requests.
lessons.objective: Coordinate fallible parallel work without confusing cancellation with joining.

cautions: SetLimit bounds active group functions, not every queued byte. All started work must be joined before its dependencies are released.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: errgroup: errors, cancellation and a real concurrency limit
strengths: Coordinate fallible parallel work without confusing cancellation with joining.
Choose one owner for submission, cancellation, joining and result publication. An error-aware group simplifies coordination but does not supply a durable transaction or every admission policy.

alternatives: Always the now-canceled group context
A new context with no owner or budget
quiz.correct: Wait ends the derived context
quiz.explanation: SetLimit bounds active group functions, not every queued byte. All started work must be joined before its dependencies are released.
quiz.hint: The derived context belongs to the group operation.
quiz.question: A successful group.Wait returns. Which context should an independent later operation use?

review.answer: Wait ends the derived context

sections.body: A group cancels its derived context when a task returns a non-nil error or when Wait returns. Keep that context inside the operation. Even a successful Wait leaves it canceled, so later independent work must use the caller’s appropriate context instead.
sections.title: Use the derived context for the owned operation
sections.walkthrough: This native function-body fragment uses the errgroup package, modern loop declarations, a preallocated output slice and a context-aware load function. The simple submission loop assumes load always exits on cancellation. The group does not deep-copy returned values.

sections.body: Go waits for room when the group is at its configured limit; that admission wait is not itself a ctx-select operation. Do not change the limit while tasks are active. TryGo can express nonblocking admission when the caller has a rejection policy. A fixed worker pool may fit a streaming or explicitly bounded queue better.
sections.title: Understand where SetLimit blocks

sections.body: Production submission may fail before every task is added. Do not return and close dependencies while already started tasks still use them. Cancel the operation and call Wait on every exit path that has launched work. Returning from a helper is not a join; a surrounding owner must enforce that lifecycle.
sections.title: Join after a submission failure

sections.body: A failed group may have populated some result slots before cancellation. Decide whether the operation permits partial success and represent it explicitly. For all-or-nothing results, return no successful result after Wait fails. Database transactions and idempotency still decide which external effects survive.
sections.title: Separate partial results from successful results

reading.takeaway: Choose one owner for submission, cancellation, joining and result publication. An error-aware group simplifies coordination but does not supply a durable transaction or every admission policy.

lessons.title: errgroup: errors, cancellation and a real concurrency limit

summary: Goroutines, channel ownership, select, buffers and who may send.
title: Concurrency
translationNote: A goroutine is not a promise and not a thread. It has no handle, no return value and no join — which is why channels and WaitGroups exist, and why "who closes this channel" is a design question rather than a detail.

lessons.explanation:
io.Reader has Read. io.Writer has Write. Files, network connections, HTTP bodies, gzip streams, strings.Reader and bytes.Buffer all satisfy one or both.

Accepting them instead of a concrete type is what makes Go code testable without mocks: the test passes a bytes.Buffer and reads the result back.

guide.caption: The same operation can use files, memory buffers or other implementations.
guide.practical: Accept interfaces that describe only the I/O behavior the function uses. A reader may return bytes and an error in the same call; process those bytes before the error. Standard helpers such as io.Copy and io.ReadAll handle the protocol details, but ReadAll uses memory proportional to the input.
guide.title: Separate the operation from the transport
guide.watchOut: Do not assume one Read fills the requested buffer. For an exact byte count, use io.ReadFull.

lessons.objective: Write a function that works on a file, a string and a test buffer.
lessons.title: Two interfaces, one method each

lessons.explanation:
encoding/json maps struct fields by name, and a tag overrides that. Only exported fields are considered, which is the first thing that catches people: a lower-case field is invisible to the encoder with no error.

Unmarshal leaves fields absent from the input untouched rather than zeroing them, so decoding into a reused struct can silently keep old values.

guide.caption: Decoding into an existing value can preserve fields absent from the input.
guide.practical: Treat tags as part of the external contract and test representative encoded values. Decode into a fresh struct when missing fields should become zero. Use a pointer field when an absent field must be distinguished from a present zero, and consider DisallowUnknownFields for strict input.
guide.title: Exported fields and tags define the wire representation
guide.watchOut: Do not silently ignore Marshal or Unmarshal errors. Lowercase fields remain invisible even if they carry a json tag.

lessons.objective: Control field names, omit empties, and know what unmarshalling leaves untouched.
lessons.question: What is printed, and where did port and secret go?
lessons.title: Struct tags are the JSON schema

lessons.explanation: Go 1.27 includes encoding/json/v2 without an experiment flag. Keeping encoding/json preserves its v1 behavior; adopting the v2 API is a separate decision. A compiling change can still alter a mobile model, persisted event or generated client. Write the expected wire representation before migrating.
lessons.objective: Compare null, empty and omitted JSON values before changing a public API.

cautions: Go compatibility does not imply that selecting different serializer defaults preserves your application protocol.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: JSON v2: migrate behavior, not just imports
strengths: Compare null, empty and omitted JSON values before changing a public API.
Preserve the established JSON contract first. Enable an intentional representation change only when fixtures and consumers agree about its meaning.

alternatives: Replace every import and trust the compiler
Make every field a string
quiz.correct: Preserve, compare, then opt in
quiz.explanation: Go compatibility does not imply that selecting different serializer defaults preserves your application protocol.
quiz.hint: A new API surface and a new wire representation are separate changes.
quiz.question: An existing endpoint must keep nil maps encoded as null during migration. Which approach fits?

review.answer: Preserve, compare, then opt in

sections.body: Ordinary nil slices and maps become empty collections under v2 defaults. V1 produces null. Neither representation is universally better: an established client may distinguish absence from an empty result. Keep fixtures for the actual exported types, including binary data and custom methods.
sections.title: Compare a zero-valued response
sections.walkthrough: The two valid JSON documents carry different collection shapes. This complete program uses only the Go 1.27 standard library. The panic checks belong to a small demonstration; an application boundary should return and classify encoding errors.

sections.body: DefaultOptionsV1 supplies the compatibility baseline through the v2 API. Later options override earlier ones, so opt into one reviewed change and keep the rest of the contract stable. A compatibility option does not validate domain data or automatically version persisted messages.
sections.title: Preserve first, opt in deliberately
sections.walkthrough: This function-body fragment imports encoding/json as jsonv1, encoding/json/v2 as jsonv2, and fmt. response is the application value. Only nil-slice formatting is deliberately changed; nil-map behavior stays at the chosen v1 baseline.

sections.body: Compare typed meaning and exact bytes separately. Sorted map output is useful for snapshots, but deterministic encoding is not a universal canonicalization format for signatures. Include old stored records, custom marshalers and independently released consumers, then stage the rollout with sampled comparisons and a format-aware rollback.
sections.title: Test old readers as well as new writers

sections.body: Keep an empty response fixture and a nonempty one. Change one option, predict the output, run both packages and explain which consumer needs the old result. The longer workshop on the website includes strict decoding, race-tested contract examples and a bounded fuzz target. It is useful preparation before a repository-wide import rewrite.
sections.title: Extend the exercise

reading.takeaway: Preserve the established JSON contract first. Enable an intentional representation change only when fixtures and consumers agree about its meaning.
