lessons.explanation:
`time.Duration` is an int64 counting nanoseconds, and the constants are what make it readable: `5 * time.Second` is a multiplication, not a function call. That is also the trap — a bare `5` is five nanoseconds, and `time.Sleep(5)` requests five nanoseconds, not five seconds. Scheduler timing may make the actual wait longer.

Two more worth knowing on sight: `end.Sub(start)` gives a Duration, and comparing Times uses Before, After and Equal rather than the operators, because a Time carries a monotonic reading as well as a wall clock.

guide.caption: A Duration is an int64 measured in nanoseconds.

nodes.detail: A plain number has no readable unit
nodes.label: Quantity

guide.practical: Use Add and Sub for instants and Before, After or Equal for comparisons. Time values may contain location and monotonic information, so == can differ from Equal. A context timeout or timer is often more useful than Sleep when the operation must be cancelable.
guide.title: Make units visible in every duration
guide.watchOut: time.Sleep(5) requests five nanoseconds; scheduling overhead determines when execution actually resumes.

lessons.objective: Write a timeout without wondering what unit it is in.
lessons.question: What does this print? Durations print themselves.
lessons.title: A Duration is a number of nanoseconds with a type

lessons.explanation:
`slices.SortFunc` takes a comparison that returns a negative number, zero or a positive one — not a bool. That trips people coming from languages where the comparator answers "is a before b". `cmp.Compare` does the right thing for any ordered type and is what the comparison should usually be built from.

For a second key, compare the first and fall through only when it is equal. That is the whole pattern, and it is worth writing out once.

guide.caption: slices.SortFunc takes a three-way comparison, not a less-than boolean.
guide.practical: Make the comparison consistent and transitive so the sorting algorithm can rely on it. Sorting changes the supplied slice in place; clone first if callers need the original order. Use SortStableFunc when equal elements must retain their original relative order.
guide.title: Compare the first key, then break ties with the second
guide.watchOut: Subtracting integers as a comparator can overflow. cmp.Compare expresses the ordering without that overflow risk.

lessons.objective: Sort a slice of structs by two keys.
lessons.title: Sorting by whatever you like

lessons.explanation:
A context is how a caller says "stop, I no longer need this". Anything that could block — a network call, a sleep, a channel receive — should take one and should select on `ctx.Done()` alongside whatever it was waiting for. A function that ignores its context is a function nothing can cancel.

`ctx.Err()` says which happened: `context.Canceled` when someone called cancel, `context.DeadlineExceeded` when the timeout ran out. Returning it directly is usually right — the caller already knows what it asked for.

guide.caption: The context carries a cancellation signal; it does not interrupt work automatically.
guide.practical: Pass context as the first parameter and propagate it to operations that already accept one. Call the returned cancel function to release resources, even if the deadline eventually expires. Keep contexts out of long-lived structs unless an API explicitly requires that lifetime.
guide.title: Cancellation has to reach the blocking operation
guide.watchOut: Do not use context values for optional arguments or general application state. Values are for request-scoped data crossing API boundaries.

lessons.objective: Make a function that waits stop waiting when told to.
lessons.title: Every blocking call should take a context

lessons.explanation:
Go's own "Writing Web Applications" tutorial and the Tour's "where to go next" both land on `http.Handler`. It is one method:

    ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)

`http.HandlerFunc` turns a function into that type. `http.ServeMux` is a Handler that dispatches to others. The sandbox has no network, so this lesson uses `httptest`: the types are real, the listen is not. A function that accepts `http.Handler` can be tested the same way in any Go module.

guide.caption: The lesson tests real handler behavior with an in-memory transport.

nodes.detail: Writes status, headers and body into the recorder
nodes.label: Handler

guide.practical: Keep HTTP behavior separate from business logic so handler tests can check methods, paths and invalid input directly. Set headers and status before writing a body; the first Write otherwise commits status 200. In GopherForge’s Wasm sandbox, httptest is the supported way to exercise these routes.
guide.title: A handler can be exercised without opening a socket
guide.watchOut: Passing an in-memory handler test does not claim that the Wasm program can bind a network socket.

lessons.objective: Serve /hello from an in-memory request, with no listen.
lessons.title: http.Handler is one method, like Reader

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's Errors page uses `strconv.Atoi` as the example of a function that returns `(int, error)`. That is the package: no `ParseInt` surprises in everyday code, no `fmt.Sscan` for a single number. `Atoi` is `ParseInt(s, 10, 0)` with a shorter name.

Failure is an error, not a panic and not a zero you are meant to guess at. Discarding that error is how `"x"` becomes port 0.

guide.caption: strconv parses representations; a numeric type conversion does not parse a string.

nodes.detail: May contain invalid or out-of-range data
nodes.label: Text input

nodes.detail: Use only after the error decision
nodes.label: Typed result

guide.practical: Use ParseInt with an explicit base and bit size when the data format requires a specific integer representation. Atoi targets int, whose width depends on the architecture. Distinguish syntax errors from out-of-range values when the user needs a useful message.
guide.title: Text parsing returns a value and a failure path
guide.watchOut: Whitespace is not automatically trimmed by Atoi. Decide whether your input contract allows it and normalize explicitly.

lessons.objective: Parse a port with Atoi and reject anything outside 1…65535.
lessons.title: strconv is how text becomes a number

lessons.explanation:
`image.Image` describes pixels through three methods: `ColorModel`, `Bounds` and `At`. A decoded PNG produces an image value; the encoded PNG file itself does not implement that interface. A type you write can implement the same pixel contract.

`image/draw` and `image/png` work with image interfaces rather than requiring one concrete bitmap type. This lesson supplies a solid rectangle with chosen bounds and color; encoding that image is a separate step.

guide.caption: An image.Image is a pixel interface, not a filename or encoded data blob.
guide.practical: Read Bounds rather than assuming every image starts at (0,0). Image implementations may be views over shared pixel storage. Rendering and encoding are separate steps: the app can display a PNG written by a program, while the Go program still uses the standard image and encoding interfaces.
guide.title: Pixels and encoded files are separate representations
guide.watchOut: A rectangle excludes Max. Iterate while x < bounds.Max.X and y < bounds.Max.Y.

lessons.objective: Implement a solid-colour image the standard library will accept.
lessons.title: image.Image is three methods, not a file

lessons.explanation: A byte slice can be a borrowed window rather than an owned result. bytes.Buffer.Bytes exposes unread storage, and Scanner.Bytes exposes a token with a limited lifetime. The type []byte does not express that lifetime. Draw the owner, the view and the next mutation before deciding whether to copy.
lessons.objective: Trace bytes.Buffer and Scanner views, then make retained results independent at a lifetime boundary.

cautions: Clip does not copy
Sending a slice does not freeze it
Reset is not secret erasure
designGuide.cost: One deliberate copy buys independent result lifetime. Measure the boundary rather than guessing from allocation count.
strengths: Borrow for immediate synchronous work
Copy only at a lifetime boundary
Document validity in the API

alternatives: Clip the view to its length
Assign the slice to a new name
quiz.correct: Copy before owner changes
quiz.explanation: Clone copies the bytes. Reset does not revoke aliases or promise to overwrite old storage. A channel send also copies a descriptor, so asynchronous consumption needs an ownership protocol.
quiz.hint: A second descriptor still refers to the same backing array.
quiz.question: A result must survive bytes.Buffer.Reset and later writes. What establishes independent ownership?

review.answer: Copy before owner changes

sections.body: Draw a row of bytes for the buffer, then a window labeled view above it. Bytes does not create a separate row. While the borrow is valid, changing an element through the view changes the buffer. A separate copy belongs on a second row with no shared storage.
sections.code:
package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
)

func main() {
    var buffer bytes.Buffer
    buffer.WriteString("alpha")
    view := buffer.Bytes()
    owned := bytes.Clone(view)
    view[0] = 'A'
    fmt.Println(buffer.String())
    buffer.Reset()
    buffer.WriteString("omega")
    fmt.Println(string(owned))
}
sections.title: One owner, one temporary view
sections.walkthrough: The output is Alpha, then alpha. The first print demonstrates aliasing before reset. bytes.Clone creates the owned result before the owner changes. The program deliberately never inspects view after reset: its old contents are not a valid result to rely on.

sections.body: Follow this order: obtain a view, consume it synchronously, then mutate or release the owner. If you must return, cache or enqueue the result beyond that boundary, copy the bytes or transfer the owner explicitly. Assigning the slice to another variable copies its descriptor and preserves sharing. Clip also keeps the existing elements shared.
sections.title: The lifetime timeline

sections.body: Scanner.Bytes may expose storage reused by the next Scan. A token consumed immediately can remain borrowed. A token saved in a collection needs its own bytes. Check Scanner.Err after the loop as a separate requirement; correct ownership does not make input parsing infallible.
sections.title: Scanner tokens need the same decision
sections.walkthrough: Each iteration copies the current token before the next Scan can replace it. The saved values therefore print red and blue. Without a copy, storing the slice descriptors would not establish a durable token contract. The final error check handles scanning failures independently.

sections.body: A successful channel send transfers the slice descriptor, not an immutable snapshot. The producer must stop using the storage until consumption finishes, or send an owned copy. For cancellation, specify who owns a buffer when enqueueing fails and who releases it after a successful handoff.
sections.title: Asynchronous work crosses the boundary

sections.body: Reset prepares a buffer for reuse and can retain its allocation. It does not guarantee erasure of sensitive bytes. Test that an owned result remains unchanged after later buffer operations. Avoid tests that require a particular stale value from an invalid view, and measure retained memory when large buffers live much longer than their input.
sections.title: Reset, retention and tests

reading.takeaway: A borrowed result is safe only within its documented lifetime. Draw the next mutation or release, then copy before that boundary when the caller needs a durable value. Test independence of valid results rather than the contents of invalid views.

lessons.title: Borrow bytes briefly; copy before their owner changes

lessons.explanation: A JSON object can omit a member, contain null, or contain a concrete zero value. Go fields alone do not always preserve those distinctions. An update that sets enabled to false must not silently become an instruction to leave enabled unchanged. Start with a state table for the operation.
lessons.objective: Choose omitempty, omitzero and request presence models from the endpoint contract.

cautions: A tag controls encoding behavior; it does not define authorization, business validation or every partial-update transition.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: JSON presence: omitted, zero and null are different states
strengths: Choose omitempty, omitzero and request presence models from the endpoint contract.
Specify presence semantics before choosing tags or pointer fields. Missing, null and a concrete zero value may represent different commands.

alternatives: Pointers always distinguish all three states
omitempty validates required input
quiz.correct: Absent and null can both become nil
quiz.explanation: A tag controls encoding behavior; it does not define authorization, business validation or every partial-update transition.
quiz.hint: Ask what a pointer contains after null and after an omitted property.
quiz.question: Ordinary decoding into a fresh *bool must distinguish missing, null and false. What is missing from that representation?

review.answer: Absent and null can both become nil

sections.body: Under v1 defaults, omitempty omits a zero integer and false boolean. Under v2 defaults those are nonempty JSON values and remain present. omitzero expresses Go zero-value omission. Do not replace tags mechanically: some response fields must be visible even when false or zero.
sections.title: Compare omission rules
sections.walkthrough: These declarations compare ordinary scalar fields. They do not describe every custom marshaler. Build table tests for zero, nonzero, nil and explicitly empty values on the actual request or response type.

sections.body: A bool stores true or false, not whether a property was absent. A *bool can distinguish absent from false in a freshly decoded value, but ordinary decoding also maps explicit null to nil. If null means clear while absence means keep, use a documented presence-aware representation or an explicit operation type.
sections.title: Do not use an ordinary bool as a PATCH protocol

sections.body: For a full replacement command, decide required fields and validate the final state. For a partial update, separately validate which transitions are allowed. Avoid reusing an already populated decoding target: fields absent from input can retain earlier state and make missing values appear supplied.
sections.title: A complete update has a simpler contract

sections.body: Test an omitted property, null, false and true independently. Assert both the final stored value and whether a write occurs. Add unknown members and malformed values to the matrix, and verify that decoding or validation failure cannot publish a partial update.
sections.title: Write the four cases before the code

reading.takeaway: Specify presence semantics before choosing tags or pointer fields. Missing, null and a concrete zero value may represent different commands.

lessons.title: JSON presence: omitted, zero and null are different states

lessons.explanation: Successful decoding proves only that input was accepted under the decoder policy. It does not authorize the caller or establish a valid business transition. V2 rejects duplicate names and invalid UTF-8 by default; exact field-name matching and unknown-member rejection are separate settings.
lessons.objective: Separate JSON syntax acceptance, unknown-member policy and domain validation.

cautions: Strict decoding cannot authorize a resource or make an external write exactly once.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: Strict JSON input: reject ambiguity before side effects
strengths: Separate JSON syntax acceptance, unknown-member policy and domain validation.
Bound input, decode under an explicit policy, validate the domain and authorize the target before performing a side effect. Test each boundary independently.

alternatives: Assume unknown names are always rejected
Compare decoder error messages only
quiz.correct: Only with the chosen strict policy
quiz.explanation: Strict decoding cannot authorize a resource or make an external write exactly once.
quiz.hint: Duplicate names and unknown names are different cases.
quiz.question: A v2 command endpoint must reject additional properties. What should its decoder do?

review.answer: Only with the chosen strict policy

sections.body: Unknown members are ignored by default in v2; use RejectUnknownMembers when the endpoint contract requires strict commands. A forward-compatible event consumer may need another policy. Bound body bytes before decoding and limit expensive domain work separately.
sections.title: Make the boundary policy visible
sections.walkthrough: The complete helper needs encoding/json/v2 aliased as jsonv2, fmt, strings and errors. Its caller must cap data size before allocation. A fresh local target prevents earlier values or a partial failed decode from becoming a successful published result.

sections.body: Use fixtures for duplicate names, differently cased names, an unknown property, invalid UTF-8, a trailing second JSON value and a blank name. Record acceptance, typed value and domain-validation result. Do not decide compatibility solely from a changed error string.
sections.title: Test syntax and business meaning separately

sections.body: A valid document or resource ID does not establish tenant access. Bind the caller scope to the authoritative lookup or update predicate. A timeout during a later external write can leave its result unknown, so strict JSON decoding is not a substitute for an idempotency protocol.
sections.title: Authorize after decoding, before acting

sections.body: For arbitrary bounded bytes, assert that failed decoding returns no usable partial value. For accepted requests, check required invariants and a typed encode/decode round trip. Seed the ambiguity cases explicitly; a ten-second campaign explores inputs without proving every future input safe.
sections.title: Fuzz a meaningful contract

reading.takeaway: Bound input, decode under an explicit policy, validate the domain and authorize the target before performing a side effect. Test each boundary independently.

lessons.title: Strict JSON input: reject ambiguity before side effects

summary: io.Reader and io.Writer, encoding/json, and testing without a framework.
title: Standard library patterns
translationNote:
Go's survey lists getting more from the standard library as a top friction. The reason is usually not missing knowledge of a package but missing knowledge of two interfaces: once io.Reader and io.Writer click, a surprising share of third-party code stops being necessary.

Some of this unit runs against in-memory transports rather than real sockets, because the sandbox has no network. The compilation and the types are real; only the transport is simulated, and every lesson says so where it applies.

lessons.explanation: Lifetime is the semantic question: how long must a value remain usable? Stack and heap placement are implementation choices used to satisfy that requirement. The compiler performs escape analysis; source syntax alone is not a dependable allocation profiler.
lessons.objective: Explain why returning a local address is safe and why allocation placement must be measured.

alternatives: The pointer always expires on the next function call
The caller must manually free the local stack frame
quiz.correct: Helps determine stack versus heap storage
quiz.explanation: Pointer syntax does not prove a heap allocation, and a value expression is not a promise of zero allocations.
quiz.hint: Separate the language lifetime guarantee from a particular allocation decision.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about escape analysis?

review.answer: Helps determine stack versus heap storage

sections.body: Returning a pointer to a local value is normal Go. The implementation arranges storage so callers do not receive a dangling pointer. Do not import C stack-lifetime rules into this code.
sections.title: A local address can safely leave a function
sections.walkthrough: The local spelling c does not disappear in a way that invalidates the returned pointer. Exactly which allocations survive optimization can depend on inlining and the surrounding call sites.

sections.body: A value receiver copies its receiver; a pointer receiver allows shared mutation and may be required by method sets. Neither form is universally faster. Large copies, escaping references, cache locality and synchronization all matter. Start with ownership and API semantics, then inspect a benchmark that represents the actual use.
sections.title: Pointers are a design decision first

sections.body: On a desktop Go installation, compiler diagnostics can report escape decisions. Their wording and decisions can change across versions; they are observations, not API guarantees.
sections.code:
go build -gcflags="-m=2" ./...
go test -bench=. -benchmem ./...
sections.title: Inspect the native build, not an assumption
sections.walkthrough: Use these commands in your development environment. Compare allocations per operation and time after warm-up. The app's WebAssembly sandbox does not reproduce every native service allocation or threading cost.

reading.takeaway: Reason about required lifetime first. Use compiler diagnostics and measurements to learn how the implementation realizes it.

lessons.title: Stacks, escape analysis and object lifetimes

lessons.explanation: Garbage collection reclaims memory that the runtime determines is no longer reachable. It does not know that an application has lost interest in a cache entry, nor does it close a forgotten network connection on a useful schedule. Ownership still matters.
lessons.objective: Follow references from roots and distinguish unreachable objects from unwanted live data.

alternatives: The garbage collector never handles byte slices
Setting any variable to nil disables future collection
quiz.correct: Stays live until its remaining references disappear
quiz.explanation: Eligible for collection does not mean the same bytes disappear from process RSS immediately.
quiz.hint: Follow every remaining reference path, including caches and blocked workers.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about a cached reachable object?

review.answer: Stays live until its remaining references disappear

sections.body: Imagine a global cache holding a pointer to an order, which points to a large receipt buffer. As long as a live reference path reaches the buffer, it is not garbage. Removing one local reference is insufficient when the cache still holds another.
sections.title: Think in reference paths
sections.walkthrough: Delete removes this map entry, not every possible reference to the order. Concurrent access to the map would require synchronization. The example focuses only on the reference graph.

sections.body: An unreachable allocation becomes eligible for reclamation; there is no promise that the operating system immediately receives the same amount of memory. Runtime-managed free space can be reused. RSS, live heap and total allocated bytes answer different questions, so compare like with like when diagnosing growth.
sections.title: Collection is not immediate destruction

sections.body: Close files and response bodies, stop owned background workers, and bound caches according to their contracts. A tracing collector can collect unreachable cycles, but it cannot make an indefinitely blocked goroutine release the values it still reaches. Avoid finalizers as normal cleanup: their timing does not establish a reliable resource protocol.
sections.title: Resources need explicit lifetime management

reading.takeaway: The GC answers reachability, not business usefulness. Remove unwanted references and close resources explicitly; then measure the correct memory metric.

lessons.title: What the garbage collector can and cannot free

lessons.explanation: A service pays for memory in more than one way: live objects occupy space, new allocations create work, and collection uses CPU. Tuning a single GC knob cannot repair an unbounded cache or a queue that retains every request body.
lessons.objective: Distinguish reducing live data from tuning collection frequency and respect a container memory limit.

alternatives: Yes, it caps every byte used by the process
Yes, it also bounds caches and request queues
quiz.correct: A soft runtime budget, not a process hard cap
quiz.explanation: The runtime memory limit is soft and cannot substitute for a bounded workload or a measured container budget.
quiz.hint: Compare allocation rate, live heap and process memory before choosing a knob.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about gomemlimit?

review.answer: A soft runtime budget, not a process hard cap

sections.body: A high allocation rate with a small live heap suggests churn: many objects become garbage quickly. A growing live heap suggests retained data or a growing workload. Capture representative profiles before changing code; removing one temporary allocation is not helpful if a cache retains gigabytes indefinitely.
sections.title: Measure two different problems

sections.body: GOGC influences the heap-growth target and therefore the tradeoff between collection frequency and memory. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft runtime memory limit, not an operating-system hard cap. Native allocations and other process memory can require additional budget. Leave measured headroom under the container limit rather than making the two numbers equal.
sections.code:
# Illustrative native-service configuration, not an iOS setting:
GOGC=100 GOMEMLIMIT=400MiB ./service
sections.title: Treat settings as tradeoffs
sections.walkthrough: The 400 MiB value is an example, not a recommendation for every 512 MiB container. Measure your binary, traffic and non-runtime memory before choosing a value.

sections.body: Avoid retaining whole request graphs in queues, bound cache entries, and reuse buffers only with clear ownership and size limits. Increasing a memory allowance may reduce collection frequency but raises memory use; forcing very frequent GC can waste CPU. A pool is an optimization with lifecycle constraints, not a guarantee that objects will stay cached or that memory use is bounded.
sections.title: Reduce work before aggressive tuning

reading.takeaway: First bound live data and measure allocation churn. Then tune collection within an observed process budget and recheck latency under load.

lessons.title: GC cost, allocation rate and memory budgets

lessons.explanation: A goroutine is a Go execution task scheduled by the runtime. An OS thread is an operating-system execution resource. The runtime multiplexes tasks onto threads; counting goroutines therefore does not tell you how many cores are doing useful work.
lessons.objective: Explain concurrency versus parallel execution without assuming a goroutine is an OS thread.

alternatives: Yes, each goroutine reserves a physical core
Yes, once the goroutine has a large enough stack
quiz.correct: Limits parallel Go execution slots, not goroutines
quiz.explanation: A low CPU percentage can coexist with severe overload caused by blocked downstream calls and growing queues.
quiz.hint: Count tasks, execution slots and operating-system threads as different quantities.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about gomaxprocs?

review.answer: Limits parallel Go execution slots, not goroutines

sections.body: In runtime terminology G represents a goroutine, M an OS thread, and P the scheduler resources needed to execute ordinary Go code. GOMAXPROCS controls how many Ps execute Go code at once. It is not a limit on total goroutines or a universal limit on all process threads.
sections.title: Use the G, M, P model carefully

sections.body: Several CPU-bound tasks need available execution capacity to run in parallel. Waiting network operations can overlap while other work proceeds. Starting ten thousand CPU-heavy goroutines does not create ten thousand cores and may add scheduling overhead. Native defaults can account for runtime and container configuration; inspect the actual service instead of copying a magic setting.
sections.code:
fmt.Println("Go execution slots:", runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0))
fmt.Println("goroutines now:", runtime.NumGoroutine())
sections.title: CPU work and waiting behave differently
sections.walkthrough: Passing zero queries the current GOMAXPROCS value. NumGoroutine is a snapshot and includes runtime/application work; it is a diagnostic signal, not a precise request counter.

sections.body: For CPU work, benchmark a bounded pool around the available CPU budget. For I/O work, use downstream concurrency, queue and deadline limits. A service can be overloaded with many waiting tasks even when CPU looks low. The iOS app's WebAssembly execution environment does not demonstrate native OS-thread behavior; these examples describe native Go services.
sections.title: Choose the right concurrency level

reading.takeaway: Goroutines express concurrency. The runtime and OS determine parallel execution within available CPU and downstream budgets.

lessons.title: Goroutines, OS threads and GOMAXPROCS

lessons.explanation: A rising memory graph is a symptom. Before changing code, ask whether traffic grew, objects are retained, workers are stuck, or allocation churn became expensive. Different diagnostic tools answer different questions.
lessons.objective: Choose a heap profile, goroutine profile, CPU profile or trace to test a specific hypothesis.

alternatives: Only the application binary size
Only the total number of source files
quiz.correct: Shows stacks that help locate blocked workers
quiz.explanation: Profiles need workload context; a large cumulative allocation total does not itself establish a live-memory leak.
quiz.hint: Pick the profile that can actually observe the suspected resource.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about a goroutine profile?

review.answer: Shows stacks that help locate blocked workers

sections.body: A heap profile helps find retained allocations; allocation profiles emphasize cumulative allocation traffic. A goroutine profile shows where tasks wait. CPU sampling identifies code consuming CPU, while an execution trace exposes scheduling and blocking relationships. Compare the same workload and interval rather than comparing unrelated snapshots.
sections.title: Choose the observation

sections.body: For a native local program, a goroutine profile can be written to a file without opening an HTTP diagnostics server. Handle the file error and close the file. Profiles can include operational details, so store and share them deliberately.
sections.title: Write a bounded diagnostic capture
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs inside an error-returning diagnostic function and imports os and runtime/pprof. Capture once at the relevant time; do not create an unbounded stream of profile files.

sections.body: If goroutine count grows after requests finish, compare stacks and identify the owner of the repeated wait. If heap grows with cache keys, inspect eviction and reference lifetimes. Change one thing and repeat the workload. A single stable run does not prove absence of races or leaks, and profiling overhead itself should be considered.
sections.title: Turn a suspicion into a comparison

reading.takeaway: Name the hypothesis, choose a tool that can observe it, and compare equivalent workloads before and after the change.

lessons.title: Find a leak by following evidence

lessons.explanation: Pooling can reduce temporary allocation, but every Get and Put creates an ownership obligation. A former owner must stop using the object after Put. A result that still aliases the object violates that obligation even when the code compiles and a small benchmark looks fast.
lessons.objective: Use sync.Pool with exclusive ownership, independent output and an explicit policy for oversized buffers.

cautions: No access after Put
No guaranteed object retention
No hard memory bound
designGuide.cost: Extra ownership protocol and possible retained capacity. Keep an unpooled baseline and discard oversized objects according to workload.
strengths: Reuse measured temporary allocation
Keep the boundary in one small function
Correct with reuse or fresh allocation

alternatives: Read it after Put if usually unchanged
Require Get to return the last object
quiz.correct: Copy before Put
quiz.explanation: Pool reuse is optional and identity is not guaranteed. An owned copy remains correct with or without reuse. A pool does not replace admission control, a bounded queue or database connection management.
quiz.hint: A later owner may reuse storage immediately; the returned value needs a separate lifetime.
quiz.question: A function returns a buffer to sync.Pool. How can its returned []byte remain safe for the caller?

review.answer: Copy before Put

sections.body: Follow Get to one active owner, then produce an independent result before Put. After release, the old owner must not read or write the buffer. The pool can discard objects and Get need not return a previously stored object, so correctness must work with both reuse and a fresh allocation.
sections.title: Draw the ownership cycle

sections.body: This encoder returns owned bytes. Its example cutoff avoids deliberately returning an oversized backing buffer to this pool. The cutoff is a workload policy, not a universal value and not a cap on total process memory.
sections.title: Copy the result before releasing its storage
sections.walkthrough: The output remains hello, Ada after another encode. bytes.Clone separates the result from temporary storage before Put. The example never assumes the second call gets the same buffer. Buffers larger than the illustrative cutoff are discarded from this reuse path, while active requests and returned results still consume memory.

sections.body: sync.Pool is not a bounded cache, a reliable queue, or a database connection manager. Objects can disappear without explicit removal. A strict concurrency limit needs admission control; a database connection needs its client library's capacity, timeout and cleanup rules. A pool alone establishes none of those contracts.
sections.title: Do not turn a pool into a resource budget

sections.body: Keep the first result, make many later calls, and verify the first bytes remain unchanged. Add parallel calls under the race detector. Do not assert that a specific object returns from Get. Test large and small inputs, and check cancellation ownership if work is queued to another goroutine.
sections.title: Test public independence, not object identity

sections.body: Compare a correct unpooled baseline against the pooled version using realistic response-size distributions. Measure allocations, retained memory and latency after bursts. Race instrumentation is for correctness checks, not production timing claims. If pooling adds complexity without a measurable benefit, keep the simpler owned-result implementation.
sections.title: Make the optimization earn its protocol

reading.takeaway: Get gives temporary exclusive access; Put ends it. Make external results independent before release, avoid identity assumptions and measure whether pooling helps. A per-object size cutoff does not bound total memory or concurrent work.

lessons.title: A pool reuses temporary objects; it does not own your results

summary: Stacks, GC, goroutines, threads and diagnostic evidence.
title: Runtime and memory
translationNote: Read worked examples without compiling. Native service behavior can differ from the app's WebAssembly execution environment.

lessons.explanation: A Go web service is more than a route callback. Every request consumes a connection, parsing work, application time and possibly downstream capacity. Give those resources explicit lifetimes. This lesson describes native server code; guest Go programs in the app cannot open network sockets.
lessons.objective: Separate request parsing, domain work, downstream deadlines and response writing.

alternatives: Owning every domain rule and database implementation
Guaranteeing a remote operation is undone after timeout
quiz.correct: Translates requests and responses around a use case
quiz.explanation: Connection-phase timeouts and a business operation deadline protect different parts of a request.
quiz.hint: Follow the request from validation to the final response, including cancellation.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about an http adapter?

review.answer: Translates requests and responses around a use case

sections.body: A handler translates a protocol into an application operation: validate input, call a service with the request context, then map the result to a response. Domain logic should not need a ResponseWriter. If the client leaves, the request context can notify cooperative downstream work.
sections.title: Keep the boundary small

sections.body: This is a native-server configuration fragment. Header and idle timeouts address specific connection phases; they are not a complete business-operation deadline. WriteTimeout must fit the response type, especially streaming, rather than being copied blindly.
sections.title: Configure a server rather than only a callback
sections.walkthrough: The values are illustrative. Add request-body limits, operation-specific deadlines and response policies based on the API. A timeout does not undo an operation the remote service already committed.

sections.body: HTTP APIs fit request/response interactions and interoperability. A batch program or local library may need no server at all. Test handlers with httptest and in-memory requests before deployment. In-memory handler tests check application behavior; they do not prove production TLS, socket, proxy or load-balancer configuration.
sections.title: Choose HTTP when it matches the problem

reading.takeaway: A handler is an adapter with explicit resource limits. Pass context into the application and test protocol behavior without requiring a running network service.

lessons.title: An HTTP request has a lifecycle and a budget

lessons.explanation: Gin supplies routing, middleware and request/response helpers on top of net/http. It is useful when those conventions reduce repeated adapter code. It does not supply your domain model, persistence policy or downstream capacity, and a small API can also use the standard library.
lessons.objective: Read route groups, path parameters and injected dependencies in a small Gin API.

alternatives: It creates a separate operating-system process for every route
It automatically implements the database layer
quiz.correct: Shares a URL prefix and middleware between routes
quiz.explanation: Gin is optional tooling around HTTP; it does not make an application architecture or network policy for you.
quiz.hint: Read the path prefix, route pattern, parameter and response in that order.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about a gin route group?

review.answer: Shares a URL prefix and middleware between routes

sections.body: New creates an engine without the default middleware set. The group applies a common path prefix. A named segment is read from the Gin context, then handed to a service. This is an illustrative fragment: store and its result/error contract are application dependencies.
sections.title: Read the route from left to right
sections.walkthrough: The application contract supplies ErrNotFound. Only that classification becomes 404; other failures are not disguised as a missing record. This fragment uses a generic 503 for dependency failure. A complete adapter should distinguish invalid input, internal faults, deadline and cancellation, use the authenticated scope in the lookup and avoid leaking internal error text.

sections.body: Construct a handler with the interface it needs, then register methods on the engine. That makes a fake store available to tests and avoids hiding process configuration in globals. Keep route names and response shapes stable as an external contract.
sections.title: Inject the dependency, not a global registry

sections.body: A Gin engine implements http.Handler, so httptest can send an in-memory request through the router and middleware. Assert status, headers and body, including errors. The app includes local-preview patterns, but these reading examples are not a promise that every Gin version or native networking feature runs in its sandbox.
sections.title: Test routing without starting a server

reading.takeaway: Use Gin to express the HTTP adapter. Keep application behavior behind explicit dependencies and test the adapter through its Handler interface.

lessons.title: Gin routes are adapters, not the whole application

lessons.explanation: Decoded JSON is not yet trusted application input. A field can have the right Go type and still violate a business rule. Bound the body, handle decoding failure, then apply domain validation before writing to storage or calling another service.
lessons.objective: Follow JSON binding, size limits, validation and a safe error response.

alternatives: The user is authorized to access every referenced record
The request is safe to retry after any side effect
quiz.correct: Does not prove authorization or every business rule
quiz.explanation: Required fields and authorization are different checks; valid JSON can still represent an invalid operation.
quiz.hint: Find the point where input first becomes allowed to cause a side effect.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about successful json binding?

review.answer: Does not prove authorization or every business rule

sections.body: This adapter accepts a JSON object with a non-empty name. ShouldBindJSON lets the handler choose its error response instead of relying on an automatically written status. The body cap is a policy example and should match the endpoint.
sections.title: Separate decoding from application rules
sections.walkthrough: The generic error avoids echoing an arbitrary decoder message. A production API can map an over-limit body to 413 and expose structured, documented field errors. Decide whether unknown JSON fields should be rejected and configure that policy deliberately.

sections.body: A valid item ID does not prove the requester may access that item. Authenticate the caller, check authorization at the relevant boundary, and keep secrets out of logs and responses. Binding tags check specified shapes; business invariants may require several fields and current state.
sections.title: Validation does not provide authorization

sections.body: Cover missing fields, wrong types, malformed and oversized input, duplicate requests and unexpected fields according to the chosen policy. Specify whether optional zero values differ from missing values. If accepting a command has an external effect, consider an idempotency contract rather than assuming retries are harmless.
sections.title: Test the cases users actually send

reading.takeaway: Decode, validate shape, enforce business rules and authorization, then perform side effects. Each step has a different responsibility.

lessons.title: Validate a request before doing side effects

lessons.explanation: Redis can be overwhelmed by too much work, large payloads, expensive commands or many clients competing for the same resources. Making every slice element a goroutine only moves pressure downstream. Treat the server, the network and the client pool as separate budgets.
lessons.objective: Distinguish client pool limits, request deadlines, rate limits and bounded command batches.

alternatives: Yes, every connection always allows exactly one request per second
Yes, it also bounds every other application instance
quiz.correct: Reuses connections; it is not a request-rate limit
quiz.explanation: A cache outage can become a database outage if fallback traffic has no admission control.
quiz.hint: Identify the client pool, the queue and the server as separate limits.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about a redis connection pool?

review.answer: Reuses connections; it is not a request-rate limit

sections.body: A shared client normally reuses connections. Creating a new client for each request defeats that reuse. A connection-pool setting is not automatically a global rate limiter, and waiting for a connection still consumes request time. Exact option semantics depend on the client version; read its production documentation.
sections.title: Understand what a client pool limits

sections.body: This native Go fragment assumes a configured shared go-redis client. Missing keys and infrastructure failures are different cases. The request context carries the parent lifetime; the shorter local timeout bounds this particular operation.
sections.title: Give each operation a bounded lifetime
sections.walkthrough: 150 ms is an example, not a universal Redis timeout. Configure and verify client network timeouts as well; do not assume a context deadline replaces every transport setting.

sections.body: Pipelining can reduce network round trips, but an enormous pipeline can increase queued work and memory. Bound batch size and total payload, avoid broad scans or expensive hot-path commands, and monitor server latency, errors, pool waits and command volume. Test fallback behavior too: when the cache slows, a sudden flood of misses can overload the database behind it.
sections.title: Batch for efficiency without removing limits

reading.takeaway: Limit work before it reaches Redis. A pool, timeout, rate limiter and bounded pipeline solve different parts of the capacity problem.

lessons.title: Redis is fast; its capacity is still finite

lessons.explanation: A cache is often added to reduce load, yet its failure path can multiply load. When a popular key expires, many callers may fetch the same value at once. When a timeout triggers retries at several layers, one user action can become many downstream operations.
lessons.objective: Design a cache-miss path that avoids multiplying identical work and ambiguous retries.

alternatives: All replicas and all Redis clients worldwide
Every completed request forever, like a persistent cache
quiz.correct: Coalesces in-flight work per key within one process
quiz.explanation: An in-flight duplicate suppressor is neither a persistent cache nor a distributed lock.
quiz.hint: Follow one expired hot key through every replica and retry layer.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about singleflight.group?

review.answer: Coalesces in-flight work per key within one process

sections.body: singleflight lets concurrent callers for the same key share one in-flight computation. The loader should have an explicit bounded lifetime. In this fragment loadCtx is owned by the service, not borrowed indefinitely from whichever request happened to arrive first.
sections.title: Collapse duplicate work within a process
sections.walkthrough: group is a shared singleflight.Group. This synchronous form waits for the shared result; callers that must independently stop waiting need a cancellation-aware design, for example DoChan with a select. Coalescing is per process, not a distributed lock across replicas.

sections.body: Choose TTLs from the data contract. Jitter can spread expirations, but it does not make stale data acceptable automatically. Serving a stale value may be useful for a catalogue and wrong for an authorization decision. Bound key count and value size, and ensure a miss cannot start unlimited fallback work.
sections.title: Define cache freshness and failure policy

sections.body: Use a small attempt budget, backoff with jitter and an overall deadline. A timed-out write may already have committed, so an automatic retry can duplicate a side effect without an idempotency contract. Coordinate retries at one layer where possible. Record attempts and final outcomes so apparent success does not conceal amplified downstream load.
sections.title: Retry only a retryable, safe operation

reading.takeaway: Coalesce duplicates, bound fallback work and retry under an explicit contract. A faster happy path does not excuse an unbounded failure path.

lessons.title: Cache misses, retries and overload amplification

summary: HTTP, Gin, Redis and the capacity of downstream services.
title: Go services
translationNote: These reading lessons explain native service designs. They do not add guest network sockets or remote services to the iOS sandbox.

lessons.explanation: Go packages provide namespaces and compile-time dependency boundaries. More packages do not automatically create a cleaner design. Start with behavior that changes together, then separate a boundary when it hides an implementation detail or makes a dependency direction clearer.
lessons.objective: Choose cohesive package boundaries and keep concrete dependencies at the edges.

cautions: A folder name does not enforce a boundary
Generic utils packages accumulate unrelated dependencies
strengths: A package has one clear reason to change
Import direction can be reviewed and tested

alternatives: In a universal package containing every database API
As a mandatory duplicate for every concrete type
quiz.correct: Names the behavior its caller needs from a dependency
quiz.explanation: A directory tree is not architecture unless dependencies and responsibilities actually follow its boundaries.
quiz.hint: Describe the caller's required behavior before naming the implementation.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about a consumer-owned interface?

review.answer: Names the behavior its caller needs from a dependency

sections.body: A package named orders can expose orders.Service or orders.Create without repeating a business prefix everywhere. A package called utils tends to accumulate unrelated dependencies because its purpose does not constrain what belongs there. Prefer a name that explains why its exported operations belong together.
sections.title: Keep names useful at the call site

sections.body: The application needs the operation Save, not every method of the database client. Define that need near the code that uses it, and inject an implementation when wiring the process.
sections.title: Let the consumer name a small interface
sections.walkthrough: The concrete SQL or Redis adapter can satisfy this interface implicitly. Do not create an interface for every struct by habit; add it where substitution or a stable boundary is useful.

sections.body: HTTP handlers can depend on application operations; those operations should not need a router context. Keep protocol and storage types from spreading through every function. An internal directory can restrict which importers may use a package, but it does not make a design cohesive by itself. Watch for import cycles as a signal that responsibilities may be entangled.
sections.title: Review dependency direction

sections.body: Start from changes the team makes together: placing an order, pricing it and persisting it. A package should expose the vocabulary needed by its callers, not its database layout. Put transport decoding in an adapter and business decisions behind a narrow application API. Draw arrows for actual Go imports: a cycle means responsibilities must move or a smaller contract must be introduced. Renaming directories to domain, service and repository does not remove coupling if every package imports one shared mutable model.
sections.code:
cmd/shop/main.go
internal/orders/service.go
internal/orders/order.go
internal/postgres/orders.go
internal/httpapi/orders.go
sections.title: Draw an import graph before a folder tree
sections.walkthrough: This is a focused layout or boundary fragment, not a second standalone program. Read it together with the complete worked example above.

sections.body: The internal directory limits which importers may use a package; it does not make methods or data private between sibling packages. Unexport identifiers that clients do not need. Keep reusable libraries outside internal only when they have real independent consumers and a compatibility policy. Avoid a util package that accumulates unrelated helpers: move a helper beside its consumer until two callers reveal one coherent abstraction. Package boundaries and module version boundaries solve different problems.
sections.title: Use internal without promising more than it enforces

sections.body: Imagine replacing Postgres with a fake for a service test. If the service imports SQL row types, the dependency crosses the intended boundary. Then imagine adding one order rule: it should be tested without HTTP. Finally inspect exported names with go doc and examine direct dependencies with go list. A good boundary makes these changes local; it does not require a dedicated interface and a separate file for every type. Record the ownership rule in package documentation so the next feature can preserve it.
sections.title: Check a boundary with a change experiment

reading.takeaway: A good boundary reduces what a caller must know. Use cohesive packages and small consumer-owned contracts where they remove real coupling.

lessons.title: Packages follow responsibilities, not a diagram

lessons.explanation: Ports and adapters is a way to keep a use case independent of delivery and infrastructure details. It is useful when one behavior has several entry points or storage implementations. The value comes from dependency direction, not from the number of folders named domain.
lessons.objective: Trace an HTTP adapter through an application operation to a storage port and compare test boundaries.

cautions: Adapters still need real integration tests
A port per field creates unnecessary indirection
flow: Application use case owns its ports
Driven adapter implements an external operation
strengths: The same use case has CLI, HTTP or test drivers
Policy should be tested without a database

alternatives: Every table and wire command used by all databases
An automatic transaction spanning unrelated external services
quiz.correct: Expresses a use case need independently of the database
quiz.explanation: Mocking a dependency tests a contract in isolation; it does not verify the concrete adapter honors that contract.
quiz.hint: Trace a single request rather than adding layers to an abstract diagram.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about a storage port?

review.answer: Expresses a use case need independently of the database

sections.body: A request body becomes a CreateOrder command. The application validates business rules and calls an OrderStore port. The HTTP adapter translates the outcome back into protocol terms. The storage adapter translates the port operation into its own database protocol. Domain rules do not inspect HTTP headers or SQL row objects.
sections.title: Trace one operation

sections.body: This example is an application fragment. Validation runs before persistence. The error receives operation context while the caller retains access to its cause.
sections.title: Keep orchestration readable
sections.walkthrough: The interface does not define transaction semantics by magic. If creating an order and publishing an event must be atomic, design that consistency boundary explicitly, for example with a database transaction and an outbox.

sections.body: A fake store can test the use case cheaply, but cannot prove that a SQL adapter writes the right schema. Add integration tests for adapters and a smaller number of end-to-end journeys. lessons.explanation: A shell starts in a working directory, and relative paths are resolved there. Before building or moving files, establish that location. These exercises use a new scratch directory on your own Mac or Linux machine; no administrator permissions are needed.
lessons.objective: Use pwd, cd, ls, mkdir, cp and mv in a small disposable workspace.

alternatives: Every file under your home directory
The path of the Go compiler executable
quiz.correct: Prints the current working directory
quiz.explanation: cd affects its own shell; another terminal can be in a different directory.
quiz.hint: Relative paths begin at the current working directory.
quiz.question: What does pwd show?

review.answer: Prints the current working directory

sections.body: pwd prints the working directory; ls -la includes hidden entries and metadata. cd changes this shell, not every terminal. The home shortcut is expanded by the shell, while a quoted path can contain spaces.
sections.code:
pwd
ls -la
cd "$HOME"
pwd
sections.title: Locate the project before changing it
sections.walkthrough: Compare the two pwd results. ls -la may show .git, but that alone does not establish a repository root. Quoting "$HOME" passes a single path, even if it contains spaces.

sections.body: mktemp -d makes a unique scratch directory. mkdir -p creates missing directory components. cp copies bytes; mv changes the path. Keep the original until you have inspected the destination rather than experimenting on project files.
sections.code:
scratch_dir=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$scratch_dir/input" "$scratch_dir/output"
printf "%s\n" "hello Go" > "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt"
cp "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/copy.txt"
mv "$scratch_dir/output/copy.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
cat "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
sections.title: Create and copy a small fixture
sections.walkthrough: The final line prints hello Go. The > operator creates or truncates the named file; it is appropriate here because the fixture is new. The scratch path stays in scratch_dir for the next command.

sections.body: wc -l counts newline-terminated lines, and cmp compares the copied content. rm removes the specifically named fixture files; rmdir removes only empty directories, making an unexpected leftover visible instead of recursively erasing it.
sections.code:
wc -l "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
cmp "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
rm "$scratch_dir/input/note.txt" "$scratch_dir/output/result.txt"
rmdir "$scratch_dir/input" "$scratch_dir/output" "$scratch_dir"
sections.title: Check the result and remove only the fixture
sections.walkthrough: wc should report one line. cmp is silent with status zero for identical files. The cleanup names only files this exercise created; rmdir fails if another file remains, so inspect rather than adding recursive deletion.

reading.takeaway: Start by checking the working directory, quote paths, and verify copied bytes before removing anything. Practice filesystem changes in a named scratch workspace, not in your only project copy.

lessons.title: Bash essentials: navigate, inspect and copy files

lessons.explanation: Most development investigations begin with a filename, a symbol or a short log fragment. Use small commands to narrow the evidence before opening a huge file. The examples assume you are in a trusted Go project and have a text application log named app.log.
lessons.objective: Combine find, grep, head, tail, sort and uniq without hiding their exit behavior.

alternatives: uniq sorts every input line itself
sort changes error messages into exit codes
quiz.correct: Groups equal lines so adjacent counts are meaningful
quiz.explanation: Do not confuse exact-line counts with rates from timestamped structured logs.
quiz.hint: uniq compares neighboring lines.
quiz.question: Why does counting repeated lines usually sort before uniq -c?

review.answer: Groups equal lines so adjacent counts are meaningful

sections.body: find selects filesystem entries; grep searches text. The quoted pattern *.go is passed to find rather than expanded by Bash. -exec passes each discovered filename as an argument, preserving spaces without parsing the output of ls.
sections.code:
find . -type f -name "*.go"
find . -type f -name "*.go" -exec grep -nH -F "ListenAndServe" {} +
sections.title: Find source files and search their content
sections.walkthrough: The first command lists Go files. The second prints filename, line number and matching text. No matches can produce a nonzero grep status; distinguish that normal search outcome from an unreadable file.

sections.body: head shows the beginning, tail the end, and tail -f follows appended data until Ctrl-C. Bound a first inspection instead of loading a multi-gigabyte file. Filtering stdout does not capture stderr from a program unless you redirect it explicitly.
sections.code:
head -n 10 app.log
tail -n 40 app.log
grep -n -F "timeout" app.log
tail -f app.log
sections.title: Read a bounded part of a log
sections.walkthrough: Stop tail -f with Ctrl-C when you have enough evidence. It does not stop the process writing the log. grep finds the literal timeout string and reports line numbers rather than interpreting it as a regular expression.

sections.body: uniq -c combines adjacent equal lines, so sort first if order does not matter. This simple pipeline counts exact repeated lines; real structured logs often contain a different timestamp per event and need field-aware parsing.
sections.code: grep -F "ERROR" app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 10
sections.title: Count repeated messages with a clear assumption
sections.walkthrough: The result is a frequency list of identical ERROR lines, not an error rate. With pipefail, an early writer can report a broken pipe when head exits; do not reuse a viewing pipeline as an unquestioned CI pass/fail gate.

reading.takeaway: Use find for paths and grep for text; quote patterns and preserve filenames as arguments. Bounded log inspection and explicit pipeline assumptions are more useful than printing every file.

lessons.explanation: Bash is useful for connecting build and deployment tools on a developer machine. Go itself does not require Bash, Docker or Kubernetes. Learning their boundaries helps when a Go program becomes part of a service workflow; these commands are reading examples, not app terminal commands.
lessons.objective: Read a small build script without splitting paths or accidentally invoking a shell through Go.

alternatives: It executes every argument as an independent shell script
It automatically authorizes any path passed by a user
quiz.correct: Preserves each element as one command argument
quiz.explanation: Avoiding a shell prevents shell reinterpretation; the invoked tool still needs an allowed-operation contract.
quiz.hint: Count arguments after expansion, especially when a path contains spaces.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about quoted bash array expansion?

review.answer: Preserves each element as one command argument

sections.body: Unquoted parameter expansion can perform word splitting and filename expansion. Quote a variable when its value should be one argument. In Bash, an array preserves several arguments without rebuilding a shell command string.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
project_dir="${1:-.}"
args=(-C "$project_dir" test ./...)
go "${args[@]}"
sections.title: Preserve a path as one argument
sections.walkthrough: With a directory containing spaces, the array still supplies one directory argument. The script uses Bash-specific array syntax; it is not a portable /bin/sh script. The -C option changes Go's working directory before running the command.

sections.body: When a Go process starts a tool, exec.Command passes an argument vector directly. This avoids asking a shell to reinterpret semicolons, substitutions or spaces. It does not by itself make the target command safe; validate its allowed operation and arguments.
sections.title: Keep data out of shell syntax
sections.walkthrough: This is native Go code for a development tool. It does not add subprocess execution to the iOS sandbox. Avoid sh -c with concatenated user input.

sections.body: A few fixed tool invocations can remain a script. Structured retries, complex state, concurrent work and testable domain rules often belong in Go. Quote "$@" when forwarding original arguments, avoid eval, and handle the exit status at the point where failure changes the workflow.
sections.title: Choose Go when the script stops being glue

reading.takeaway: Preserve argument boundaries. Use Bash for small orchestration and direct process argument vectors from native Go when no shell language is needed.

lessons.title: Bash passes arguments; quoting defines their boundaries

lessons.explanation: A script is another program with success and failure paths. A command printing plausible output can still fail. Pipelines complicate this because the last command can succeed even when an earlier producer failed.
lessons.objective: Read pipeline failure behavior and keep configuration and secrets out of command strings.

alternatives: tee reruns every failed Go test automatically
A pipeline always ignores the last command's status
quiz.correct: Makes upstream failure affect the pipeline status
quiz.explanation: set -e has contextual exceptions; an explicit failure branch is often easier to reason about.
quiz.hint: Check which command supplies the pipeline's status before trusting its output.
quiz.question: Which statement is correct about bash pipefail?

review.answer: Makes upstream failure affect the pipeline status

sections.body: Bash pipefail makes a pipeline fail when a component fails, instead of using only the final command's status. Check that status explicitly at the workflow boundary. set -e has exceptions in conditionals and other constructs, so it is not a replacement for understanding control flow.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u -o pipefail
if go test ./... | tee test.log; then
    printf "%s\n" "Tests passed"
else
    printf "%s\n" "Tests failed; inspect test.log" >&2
    exit 1
fi
sections.title: Observe the whole pipeline
sections.walkthrough: tee preserves a log while showing output. With pipefail, a failing go test makes the condition fail even when tee succeeds. This script is for a trusted local project and writes one named log file.

sections.body: A prefix assignment belongs to one child process; export passes a variable to later children from this shell. Check selected non-secret settings instead of dumping the full environment. Already-running services keep their original environment.
sections.code:
APP_ENV=development go run ./cmd/api
export APP_ENV=development
printf "APP_ENV=%s\n" "$APP_ENV"
command -v go
sections.title: Pass configuration and inspect one setting
sections.walkthrough: The first line runs a foreground API until you stop it; execute the following commands after it exits or in another shell. The example assumes cmd/api exists and does not require a credential. command -v shows which Go executable Bash will resolve.

sections.body: A trap can arrange cleanup of resources a script created, but it cannot roll back an external side effect automatically. Avoid rerunning a deployment simply because its status command timed out. Keep a stable operation identifier and inspect the outcome before retrying. As a script grows, move complex state transitions into a program with tests.
sections.title: Make cleanup and retries deliberate

reading.takeaway: A successful last pipeline command does not prove upstream success. Preserve exit status, handle failure explicitly, and avoid exposing configuration secrets.

lessons.title: Pipelines, exit codes and explicit failure handling

lessons.explanation: A process has a PID, an exit status and open streams. Starting a service in the background does not detach it from responsibility: keep the PID and wait for completion. These commands assume a local Go project with cmd/api and an available port.
lessons.objective: Start one Go service, retain its PID, send TERM and wait for its result.

alternatives: Kills every process named api
Retries the last failed network request
quiz.correct: Observes completion and collects the child exit status
quiz.explanation: A PID can be reused after exit; keep ownership instead of targeting processes by vague names.
quiz.hint: Background work still has an outcome.
quiz.question: What does wait "$api_pid" do for a child started in this shell?

review.answer: Observes completion and collects the child exit status
review.prompt: Bash wait with a child PID

sections.body: Build first, then run the binary itself in the background. $! is the PID of the latest asynchronous command. A background go run process may introduce a build/launcher process, so it is a poor substitute when practicing exact signal ownership.
sections.code:
mkdir -p bin
go build -o ./bin/api ./cmd/api
./bin/api > api.log 2>&1 &
api_pid=$!
printf "API PID: %s\n" "$api_pid"
sections.title: Start the binary you can stop directly
sections.walkthrough: Run the launch only after the build succeeds. Both output streams go to api.log. Record this PID instead of searching all processes by a broad application name or terminating unrelated Go jobs.

sections.body: ps reports process state; kill -0 checks that a PID can be addressed without sending a signal. lsof is a separately installed utility on some systems and can identify a listening socket; it does not prove the HTTP handler returns useful responses.
sections.code:
ps -p "$api_pid" -o pid,etime,args
kill -0 "$api_pid"
lsof -nP -iTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN
sections.title: Inspect the process and the listening port
sections.walkthrough: Check that the socket belongs to the binary you launched. If lsof is missing, use your OS socket inspection tool. A process may exit between any two commands; observation is not a lifetime guarantee.

sections.body: TERM lets a cooperative service drain work. wait observes your shell child and reaps it; an if branch can preserve nonzero status without aborting the shell. SIGKILL prevents application cleanup, so use it only after diagnosing an unresponsive process.
sections.code:
kill -TERM "$api_pid"
if wait "$api_pid"; then
    printf "%s\n" "Service exited successfully"
else
    status=$?
    printf "Service exit status: %s\n" "$status"
fi
tail -n 20 api.log
sections.title: Request shutdown and collect the outcome
sections.walkthrough: A graceful service can return zero. A process terminated by a signal may report a nonzero status; inspect its log and shutdown contract. wait works for children of this shell, not any arbitrary PID from another terminal.

reading.takeaway: Keep the child PID, inspect it, request TERM and wait for the outcome. A listening port, a live process and a successful HTTP response are three different observations.

lessons.title: Processes, signals and exit status

lessons.explanation: A useful script has explicit inputs and predictable cleanup. Bash distinguishes positional arguments, shell variables and exported environment. This lesson puts those pieces into a small test wrapper instead of assuming that adding set -e makes every failure path correct.
lessons.objective: Read required configuration, forward quoted arguments and clean a temporary workspace with a trap.

alternatives: Already running services receive the new value immediately
The value becomes a Kubernetes Secret
quiz.correct: Passes a variable to subsequently launched child processes
quiz.explanation: Configuration is not automatically secret; command traces and logs can reveal it.
quiz.hint: A child receives an environment when it starts.
quiz.question: What changes when you export APP_ENV?

review.answer: Passes a variable to subsequently launched child processes

sections.body: ${1:-.} supplies a default when the first argument is absent or empty. A prefix assignment affects one command environment; export affects later child processes from this shell. Neither changes an already running service.
sections.code:
project_dir="${1:-.}"
printf "Testing: %s\n" "$project_dir"
GOMAXPROCS=2 go -C "$project_dir" test ./...
export APP_ENV=development
printf "APP_ENV=%s\n" "$APP_ENV"
sections.title: Read arguments and pass a setting to one process
sections.walkthrough: The Go -C flag precedes the test command. The temporary GOMAXPROCS assignment does not permanently change your shell. Never print the complete environment to diagnose one non-secret setting.

sections.body: The : command with ${name:?message} reports a required input. mktemp creates the workspace, and EXIT runs cleanup on ordinary shell termination. The script forwards "$@" as separate arguments and uses an explicit test branch to preserve failure.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
: "${PROJECT_DIR:?Set PROJECT_DIR to a Go project}"
work_dir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
trap 'rm -f "$work_dir/test.log"; rmdir "$work_dir"' EXIT
if go -C "$PROJECT_DIR" test "$@" ./... > "$work_dir/test.log" 2>&1; then
    cat "$work_dir/test.log"
else
    cat "$work_dir/test.log" >&2
    exit 1
fi
sections.title: Validate inputs and clean only owned temporary data
sections.walkthrough: Save this as check.sh and call it with bash, PROJECT_DIR set, and optional go test flags such as -count=1. The trap names the one file it owns. SIGKILL and machine failure cannot run shell cleanup.

sections.body: bash -n parses without executing the script; it does not prove that command names, paths or remote systems exist. --help or command -v can establish what is installed. Review changes before making a script executable or putting it into CI.
sections.code:
bash -n check.sh
command -v bash
command -v go
PROJECT_DIR="$PWD" bash check.sh -count=1
sections.title: Check syntax before running the script
sections.walkthrough: Syntax success is silent. The final line runs tests and can download required Go modules; it is an execution step, not another parser check. Keep credentials out of arguments and traces such as bash -x.

reading.takeaway: A script should declare its inputs, preserve argument boundaries and clean only resources it created. Parsing, executing and validating its external effects are separate checks.

lessons.title: Small scripts: arguments, environment and cleanup

lessons.explanation: Git records snapshots, not a magic backup of every unsaved editor buffer. Start in an existing local repository and inspect your changes. The sequence below makes a topic branch, stages one reviewed path and records a local commit; publishing comes in the next lesson.
lessons.objective: Keep working tree, staging area and committed history distinct.

alternatives: Only untracked files not yet added
Every commit already pushed to every remote
quiz.correct: Shows the snapshot changes queued for the next commit
quiz.explanation: git restore --staged preserves the working file; plain git restore can replace it.
quiz.hint: The staging area is the next snapshot.
quiz.question: Which changes does git diff --staged show?

review.answer: Shows the snapshot changes queued for the next commit

sections.body: git status --short summarizes tracked and untracked paths. git diff shows unstaged tracked changes; git diff --staged shows what the next commit contains. Untracked file content is not included in ordinary git diff.
sections.code:
git status --short
git diff -- main.go
git diff --staged
git log -5 --oneline
sections.title: Inspect before selecting a change
sections.walkthrough: Compare the two diff views. A file can have both staged and unstaged edits, and the next commit includes only the staged snapshot. -- separates options/revisions from the path main.go.

sections.body: switch -c creates and selects a new branch at the current commit. add stages the named content. Inspect the staged result before committing, rather than using add . when a repository includes unrelated experiments or local credentials.
sections.code:
git switch -c feature/health-check
git add -- main.go
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add health endpoint"
sections.title: Put a reviewed change on a topic branch
sections.walkthrough: Use an unused branch name and a real main.go change. The commit remains local until you push it. If a hook fails, inspect its output and rerun the necessary check rather than bypassing it automatically.

sections.body: restore --staged changes the index back toward HEAD while leaving the working file intact. A plain restore of the working tree has a different, destructive meaning. Check both views after unstaging to make the distinction visible.
sections.code:
git restore --staged -- main.go
git status --short
git diff -- main.go
sections.title: Unstage without discarding your edit
sections.walkthrough: Use this on a staged change before committing. Your edits should now be unstaged. This is not a command to undo an existing commit; history repair and reverting a published change are different operations.

reading.takeaway: Review unstaged and staged diffs separately, stage intended paths and commit on a named branch. Unstaging an edit preserves it; overwriting the working tree may discard it.

lessons.title: Git daily work: inspect, branch, stage and commit

lessons.explanation: A remote-tracking branch is your local record of a remote branch at the last fetch. Fetching updates that record without integrating it into your current branch. The examples assume an origin remote, a main branch and an existing topic branch you own.
lessons.objective: Inspect upstream changes before integration and keep unfinished work recoverable.

alternatives: It merges origin/main into every local branch
It publishes all uncommitted files
quiz.correct: Updates remote-tracking refs without merging into HEAD
quiz.explanation: A rejected push should lead to comparison, not an automatic forced history rewrite.
quiz.hint: Fetch and integration are separate operations.
quiz.question: What does git fetch origin normally update?

review.answer: Updates remote-tracking refs without merging into HEAD

sections.body: remote -v shows fetch and push destinations; inspect those before publishing. fetch origin updates remote-tracking references. The three-dot diff compares the topic branch against its merge base with origin/main, highlighting the branch contribution.
sections.code:
git remote -v
git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main
git diff origin/main...HEAD
sections.title: Fetch and compare before merging
sections.walkthrough: HEAD..origin/main lists commits reachable from origin/main but not HEAD. Fetch does not change your working files. A remote URL may contain sensitive information; avoid pasting it indiscriminately into public logs.

sections.body: stash push -u includes untracked files as well as tracked edits, but not ignored files by default. apply restores a stash while retaining its saved entry. Inspect and resolve any conflicts before deciding to drop the saved copy.
sections.code:
git stash push -u -m "WIP before syncing"
git stash list
git stash show --stat "stash@{0}"
git stash apply "stash@{0}"
git status --short
sections.title: Temporarily store an unfinished tracked change
sections.walkthrough: Only apply when a stash entry actually exists. apply can conflict; it does not mean every file was restored cleanly. The retained stash is useful until the restored work is checked. A stash is local, not a shared backup.

sections.body: On a clean main branch, pull --ff-only refuses an implicit merge when histories diverge. A topic branch push sets its upstream without rewriting remote history. A rejected push is evidence to fetch and inspect, not a reason to force-push blindly.
sections.code:
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git switch feature/health-check
git push -u origin feature/health-check
sections.title: Integrate deliberately and publish the branch
