sections.title: Recover without a retry storm

reading.takeaway: Bound admission and waiting as well as sockets, then tune using correlated request, pool and query evidence. More connections do not repair an overloaded database.

lessons.title: MongoDB under load: budget waiting before enlarging the pool

lessons.explanation: Redis is often used as a low-latency data-structure service, but the network, client pool and command cost still exist. Create a shared client, keep a bounded operation context and distinguish redis.Nil from transport failures. A missing optional cache entry and an unavailable required store have different application contracts.
lessons.objective: Configure go-redis deadlines, connection budgets and explicit cache-miss behavior.

cautions: redis.Nil from GET means this key is absent. A transport failure is a different result; unlimited fallback work during an outage can overwhelm the origin.
designGuide.cost: Shared pools save connection setup; their total size, retries and waiting must fit the deployment’s capacity budget.
strengths: Configure go-redis deadlines, connection budgets and explicit cache-miss behavior.

alternatives: Treat both as evidence that Redis lost every key
Assume both guarantee an origin database request will be cheap
quiz.correct: Means the key is absent, not a connection outage
quiz.explanation: redis.Nil from GET means this key is absent. A transport failure is a different result; unlimited fallback work during an outage can overwhelm the origin.
quiz.hint: Choose behavior for each error class.
quiz.question: How should a GET cache miss differ from a transport error?

review.answer: Means the key is absent, not a connection outage

sections.body: This lesson uses github.com/redis/go-redis/v9 with v9.16.0 as an example pin. PoolSize and MaxActiveConns are distinct knobs; do not assume a pool’s preferred retained size is a universal hard ceiling. Confirm options against the pinned version rather than copying future-version defaults.
sections.title: Construct one client with explicit example budgets
sections.walkthrough: The values illustrate a bounded small-client configuration, with automatic retries disabled so policy is visible. Production TLS, authentication and addresses come from configuration; re-enable suitable retries only with an overall operation budget and duplicate-effect analysis.

sections.body: redis.Nil represents a missing key for a GET, not a dead server. Preserve other errors so a caller can apply the intended fallback or failure policy. A fallback that recomputes expensive data on every transport failure can overwhelm the primary database during a Redis outage.
sections.title: Handle absence explicitly
sections.walkthrough: This is a helper returning string and error. The application supplies a bounded ctx and loadFromOrigin; the example deliberately surfaces infrastructure failure instead of silently starting unlimited origin requests.

sections.body: Later client versions can change pooling and pipeline behavior. Pin and test the version used by the service, including cancellation and saturation. These native network examples are not executable Redis access inside the app’s WASI sandbox; they teach the surrounding Go service environment.
sections.title: Keep version and workload assumptions visible

reading.takeaway: Reuse the client, configure bounded waiting and handle value, miss and outage separately. Fallback and retry behavior are application decisions, not invisible conveniences.

lessons.title: Redis: share the client and distinguish a miss from an outage

lessons.explanation: A cache duplicates another source of truth, so freshness and ownership must be explicit. Cache-aside reads can miss together, all query the origin and then repopulate the same key. TTL bounds one kind of staleness; it does not prevent a stampede or make a read-modify-write sequence correct.
lessons.objective: Design expiry, invalidation, negative caching and stampede control deliberately.

cautions: In-process coalescing does not coordinate other replicas or make invalidation races disappear.
designGuide.cost: Caching adds duplicate state, invalidation and miss coordination; measure saved origin work against stale-data risk.
strengths: Design expiry, invalidation, negative caching and stampede control deliberately.

alternatives: Only a longer TTL on keys that have not been created yet
One unlimited goroutine for every origin request
quiz.correct: Does not prevent misses from flooding the origin
quiz.explanation: In-process coalescing does not coordinate other replicas or make invalidation races disappear.
quiz.hint: Consider the empty-cache path, including all replicas.
quiz.question: What extra protection does a cache-aside loader need during a burst of misses?

review.answer: Does not prevent misses from flooding the origin

sections.body: Use one SET operation with expiry when creating an expiring value. A separate SET followed by EXPIRE leaves a failure window where the key can survive without the intended lifetime. An ordinary later SET can also change existing TTL behavior, so decide the overwrite policy.
sections.code:
redis-cli SET demo:product:42 '{"name":"tea"}' EX 60
redis-cli GET demo:product:42
redis-cli TTL demo:product:42
sections.title: Set value and expiration together
sections.walkthrough: Run against an isolated development Redis using the demo namespace. TTL reports remaining expiry state, not freshness relative to a database update that happened after the value was cached.

sections.body: Coalesce identical in-process fills and independently bound the total number of origin calls. A per-key singleflight group only coordinates callers in this process; many service replicas can still miss together. Optional TTL jitter spreads expirations but does not guarantee a global rate limit.
sections.title: Bound concurrent misses
sections.walkthrough: The fragment shows the atomic value-plus-expiry client operation after an origin load. It does not implement coalescing or cross-process coordination; those policies belong to the loader boundary and must be tested separately.

sections.body: Negative caching can reduce repeated absent-item lookups, but use a short deliberate lifetime and a representation distinct from a real value. A database update followed by cache deletion can race with an older in-flight fill. Use versioned keys or another coherent invalidation design when that stale-write window is unacceptable.
sections.title: Handle stale and missing data as distinct cases

reading.takeaway: Set TTL atomically, bound origin fills and define the acceptable stale window. TTL, coalescing and invalidation address different failure modes.

lessons.title: Redis cache-aside: TTLs do not solve concurrent fills

lessons.explanation: Pipelining lets a client send multiple commands without waiting for every individual round trip. It can improve throughput for independent work, but it does not make the group indivisible. Large batches also retain commands and replies in memory and can worsen latency for other work.
lessons.objective: Bound command batches, inspect command errors and separate batching from atomicity.

cautions: MULTI/EXEC does not roll back already executed commands after a runtime command error.
designGuide.cost: Batches reduce network round trips while retaining command/reply memory and increasing ambiguous partial-outcome work.
strengths: Bound command batches, inspect command errors and separate batching from atomicity.

alternatives: Every earlier write rolls back if a later command errors
No other client can execute a command between its commands
quiz.correct: Batches round trips without making the group atomic
quiz.explanation: MULTI/EXEC does not roll back already executed commands after a runtime command error.
quiz.hint: Transport batching and a transactional boundary are different.
quiz.question: What does pipelining guarantee about the whole batch?

review.answer: Batches round trips without making the group atomic

sections.body: Queue a small known batch and inspect the returned command objects. An error from Exec needs interpretation alongside each command result. A connection failure can leave the caller uncertain which writes the server executed; a batch is not an automatic rollback boundary.
sections.title: Batch independent work
sections.walkthrough: This fragment batches two independent reads and tolerates missing keys explicitly. A write pipeline needs its own partial-outcome and retry policy; replaying all writes after an ambiguous error can duplicate effects.

sections.body: MULTI/EXEC groups commands atomically with respect to interleaving, but runtime command errors do not provide relational-database rollback. WATCH adds optimistic checks and can require a whole retry. A Lua script can perform a short conditional transition, but expensive scripts block other work on the server execution path.
sections.code:
redis-cli <<'REDIS'
MULTI
SET demo:a 1
INCR demo:count
EXEC
REDIS
sections.title: Choose atomicity separately
sections.walkthrough: The heredoc sends all commands through one redis-cli connection against an isolated development instance. Starting separate redis-cli processes for MULTI and EXEC would not create one transaction; connection ownership is part of the protocol.

sections.body: Cap commands and total encoded bytes, not only the number of business items. Measure batch duration, reply sizes and tail latency while other clients work. Client versions may use separate pipeline pools, so inspect the pinned version when calculating deployment-wide connection limits.
sections.title: Set a memory and latency budget for batches

reading.takeaway: Batch bounded independent work to reduce round trips, and choose atomicity and retry semantics explicitly. Inspect partial outcomes rather than assuming Exec implies rollback.

lessons.title: Redis pipelines save round trips; they are not transactions

lessons.explanation: A counter with a timeout and a temporary ownership key look small, but concurrent requests and pauses expose their failure windows. Put dependent steps in one short atomic transition and distinguish an expired lease from a durable guarantee that only one worker can ever act.
lessons.objective: Avoid split increment/expiry races and unsafe lock deletion.

cautions: Expiry changes the Redis key, not the execution state of an old process. A paused former owner can resume after a new owner starts; the protected resource may need fencing.
designGuide.cost: Atomic scripts add protocol and recovery complexity; a lease is weaker than a durable resource-side ownership guarantee.
strengths: Avoid split increment/expiry races and unsafe lock deletion.

alternatives: Redis pauses every process that previously held the key
A unique token prevents all network failures
quiz.correct: Does not stop a paused former owner from continuing
quiz.explanation: Expiry changes the Redis key, not the execution state of an old process. A paused former owner can resume after a new owner starts; the protected resource may need fencing.
quiz.hint: A key’s lifetime and a process’s execution lifetime differ.
quiz.question: Why can a resource still need fencing after a lease expires?

review.answer: Does not stop a paused former owner from continuing

sections.body: INCR followed by EXPIRE in separate operations can leave a counter without expiry if the client fails between them. A short script can attach expiry only when the counter is first created. This is an anchored fixed-window example, not a smooth sliding-window limiter.
sections.code:
counter := redis.NewScript(`
local n = redis.call("INCR", KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
return n
`)
n, err := counter.Run(ctx, rdb, []string{"demo:rate"}, 1000).Int64()
if err != nil { return err }
if n > 100 { return ErrLimited }
sections.title: Make a fixed-window counter transition atomic
sections.walkthrough: The go-redis script API passes one explicitly named development key and a positive window in milliseconds. This example permits 100 events in a window anchored at the first increment; ErrLimited is an application error. Define unavailable-store behavior separately.

sections.body: SET key token NX PX can create a temporary lease. Release by checking the stored token and deleting in the same atomic operation, not by a GET and later DEL. Generate a unique token for each acquisition; a stale owner must not remove a new owner’s lease.
sections.code:
release := redis.NewScript(`
local current = redis.call("GET", KEYS[1])
if current == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
end
return 0
`)
// token is unique to this successful SET key token NX PX acquisition.
deleted, err := release.Run(ctx, rdb, []string{key}, token).Int64()
if err != nil { return err }
_ = deleted // 0 means the lease no longer belongs to this acquisition.
sections.title: A lease must be released only by its owner
sections.walkthrough: The script compares the acquisition token inside the server before deletion. It solves that release race, but a paused worker may still continue after its lease expires; a protected resource may need fencing or another stronger ownership mechanism.

sections.body: An acknowledgment can be lost, a lease can expire during a pause and failover can change which writes survive. A Redis key alone is not a proof of exclusive business execution across failures. Use resource-side idempotency, version checks or fencing when duplicate work could violate an invariant.
sections.title: Explain the failure model before calling it a lock

reading.takeaway: Make dependent counter steps atomic and release leases by token. Design the downstream invariant for pauses, ambiguity and expired ownership.

lessons.title: Redis counters and leases need atomic transitions and ownership

lessons.explanation: A consumer group tracks delivery and acknowledgment, not automatic exactly-once application effects. A worker may crash after updating another database but before XACK. Redelivery is useful recovery, so the handler must recognize an operation it has already applied.
lessons.objective: Understand consumer groups, pending entries, redelivery and bounded retention.

cautions: The effect may commit before a worker crashes without acknowledging. Redelivery can then repeat it; pending-entry recovery needs destination-side idempotency.
designGuide.cost: Consumer groups need retention, pending-work recovery, idempotent effects and explicit storage durability.
strengths: Understand consumer groups, pending entries, redelivery and bounded retention.

alternatives: Consumer groups roll back all external databases on failure
Reading with > guarantees an entry is delivered only once forever
quiz.correct: Can cause redelivery after an effect already happened
quiz.explanation: The effect may commit before a worker crashes without acknowledging. Redelivery can then repeat it; pending-entry recovery needs destination-side idempotency.
quiz.hint: The worker can fail between the effect and acknowledgment.
quiz.question: Why must a stream consumer make its external effect idempotent?

review.answer: Can cause redelivery after an effect already happened

sections.body: In an isolated development instance, create a stream and group and append a demonstration event. XREADGROUP with > asks for new entries for this group. Acknowledge only after the application’s durable effect succeeds.
sections.code:
redis-cli XGROUP CREATE demo:events workers 0 MKSTREAM
redis-cli XADD demo:events '*' operationID order-42 kind created
redis-cli XREADGROUP GROUP workers worker-1 COUNT 10 STREAMS demo:events '>'
sections.title: Read new entries with one group
sections.walkthrough: Replace worker names per process and retain the stream entry ID returned by the read. The demonstration group starts from 0 intentionally; starting at $ instead changes whether existing history is delivered.

sections.body: A delivered but unacknowledged entry remains pending for the group. Inspect pending work and use a supported reclaim mechanism after an appropriate idle threshold. A slow healthy worker and a dead worker can look alike, so claiming work must not assume the old consumer has physically stopped.
sections.code:
redis-cli XPENDING demo:events workers
redis-cli XAUTOCLAIM demo:events workers worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
# After the effect succeeds, acknowledge its actual returned entry ID:
# redis-cli XACK demo:events workers 1710000000000-0
sections.title: Inspect and reclaim pending entries
sections.walkthrough: XAUTOCLAIM requires a compatible server version and returns a continuation cursor as well as claimed entries. Iterate with explicit work bounds; the sample acknowledgment ID is a placeholder, not a success shortcut.

sections.body: Deduplicate the operation at the durable destination and treat replay as a normal path. Configure stream trimming so it does not discard work that still matters to consumers. Acknowledgment does not itself specify Redis persistence, replication acknowledgment or recovery guarantees; test those separately for the deployment.
sections.title: Keep delivery, retention and durability distinct

reading.takeaway: Acknowledge after a durable idempotent effect, recover pending work deliberately, and budget retention and storage independently of consumer-group delivery.

lessons.title: Redis Streams: acknowledge after the durable effect

lessons.explanation: Redis command latency can rise because of expensive commands, a hot key, big values, persistence work, network delay or waiting in the client. A low average hides queues and timeout bursts. Correlate request errors with server and client evidence before increasing goroutines or connection limits.
lessons.objective: Inspect server latency and memory while bounding client work and retry amplification.

cautions: SLOWLOG measures server execution. Callers can still wait for a client connection or network response; retries can then amplify load or repeat an ambiguous write.
designGuide.cost: Latency and eviction policies trade memory, availability and persistence work; client concurrency cannot remove a hot-key bottleneck.
strengths: Inspect server latency and memory while bounding client work and retry amplification.

alternatives: Redis always measures the full HTTP request path
SCAN COUNT imposes an exact global rate limit
quiz.correct: Does not exclude client-pool or network latency
quiz.explanation: SLOWLOG measures server execution. Callers can still wait for a client connection or network response; retries can then amplify load or repeat an ambiguous write.
quiz.hint: Locate waiting before and after server command execution.
quiz.question: Why can callers time out while SLOWLOG shows no slow commands?

review.answer: Does not exclude client-pool or network latency

sections.body: In an authorized development environment, inspect memory, command statistics and recent slow commands. SLOWLOG measures server command execution, not every network or client-pool delay. Keep raw keys and command arguments out of broadly shared diagnostics when they may contain user data.
sections.code:
redis-cli INFO memory
redis-cli INFO stats
redis-cli INFO commandstats
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10
redis-cli LATENCY LATEST
sections.title: Use focused observation commands
sections.walkthrough: Metrics and latency monitoring availability depend on server configuration and permissions. Compare the same time window with client pool wait and request p99; a quiet SLOWLOG does not prove that callers were fast.

sections.body: KEYS can block while traversing a large keyspace. SCAN divides that work into cursor-driven steps, but it is not a snapshot, COUNT is a hint and keys may appear more than once. Keep downstream handling idempotent and avoid moving all returned keys into one giant slice.
sections.code:
redis-cli SCAN 0 MATCH 'demo:*' COUNT 100
# Continue with the returned cursor until it is 0.
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE demo:product:42
sections.title: Scan incrementally and cap batch work
sections.walkthrough: A single SCAN call is not a complete inventory. Even incremental maintenance needs rate and time budgets; do not run an unbounded sweep simply because each individual command looks small.

sections.body: Eviction policy and persistence determine whether a value can disappear and what survives failure. Replication is not automatically synchronous durability. Retrying INCR after a lost response may apply the effect twice; use an operation identifier and a suitable atomic protocol when duplicate effects are unacceptable. Bound retries within one deadline and measure recovery after overload.
sections.title: Define storage and retry guarantees

reading.takeaway: Separate client wait from server execution, keep maintenance incremental and design for eviction, persistence and ambiguous write outcomes. More concurrency is not a repair for a hot bottleneck.

translationNote: Read worked native-service examples here. Run them against an isolated development database on your own machine; these lessons do not add network sockets to the app sandbox.

lessons.explanation: sql.DB is a concurrency-safe pool handle, not a single database connection. Reuse it across the application and close it after its users drain. These lessons describe native Go services using a real driver; the app’s bounded WASI programs cannot open remote database sockets.
lessons.objective: Configure database/sql as a shared pool and measure its actual pressure.

cautions: A larger connection cap can move waiting into an overloaded database. Admission and query efficiency still need their own policies.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL: one pool, explicit capacity and observable waiting
strengths: Configure database/sql as a shared pool and measure its actual pressure.
Own one shared pool, bound operation lifetimes and admission, and measure pool waits across all replicas before changing connection limits.

alternatives: Only one replica’s connection count
The number of Go source files
quiz.correct: A shared pool, not one connection
quiz.explanation: A larger connection cap can move waiting into an overloaded database. Admission and query efficiency still need their own policies.
quiz.hint: Multiply per-process settings by every active pool owner.
quiz.question: Fifty replicas each allow twelve connections. Which budget must be checked before scaling further?

review.answer: A shared pool, not one connection

sections.body: sql.Open generally constructs a handle rather than proving connectivity. Use a bounded PingContext for startup evidence, then handle every operation error separately. Configure a reviewed driver version in the native service module; pgx/v5/stdlib is one PostgreSQL driver option.
sections.title: Construct once and verify readiness
sections.walkthrough: This startup-function fragment imports database/sql, context, fmt, time and the chosen PostgreSQL driver registration. The DSN comes from configuration. The numeric settings are examples, not sizing advice; a returned shared pool needs one application lifetime owner.

sections.body: A limit of twelve per replica means something different with two replicas than with fifty. Reserve database capacity for migrations, administration and other applications. SetMaxOpenConns bounds this pool’s open connections; it is not a global request limiter or a cap on goroutines waiting to acquire one.
sections.title: Budget across the deployment

sections.body: DB.Stats exposes OpenConnections, InUse, Idle, WaitCount and WaitDuration. Wait counters accumulate, so compare their changes over the same measurement interval. A high wait rate can reflect slow transactions, leaked rows or too much admission rather than a pool that should simply be enlarged.
sections.code:
stats := db.Stats()
fmt.Println(stats.OpenConnections, stats.InUse, stats.Idle)
fmt.Println(stats.WaitCount, stats.WaitDuration)
// Record deltas over a defined interval alongside request latency.
sections.title: Read counters as changes over an interval
sections.walkthrough: The fragment observes a shared sql.DB and imports fmt. Lifetime counters do not identify the present bottleneck by themselves. Correlate a pool-wait interval with query latency, queue length, errors and the database’s own evidence.

sections.body: A native pgxpool.Pool is another pool abstraction with its own settings and metrics. Do not wrap one pool in another or assume database/sql option names apply unchanged. Choose the API the service uses, then test saturation and shutdown for that actual combination.
sections.title: Distinguish other pool APIs

reading.takeaway: Own one shared pool, bound operation lifetimes and admission, and measure pool waits across all replicas before changing connection limits.

lessons.explanation: A successful QueryContext does not mean every row will decode successfully. Network and server errors can occur during iteration, and Scan can fail on a type or null mismatch. Decide whether partial results are meaningful; do not silently return a successful incomplete list.
lessons.objective: Write a cancellation-aware query loop without losing iteration failures.

cautions: A parameterized tenant value still requires authorization, and LIMIT is not a universal bound on query execution cost.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL rows: close, check errors and bound the result
strengths: Write a cancellation-aware query loop without losing iteration failures.
Check Query, Scan and final iteration errors as separate phases. Close owned rows, authorize scope and cap returned work before reporting a successful result.

alternatives: Return three records with no error
Ignore the final iteration status
quiz.correct: Rows.Err after the loop
quiz.explanation: A parameterized tenant value still requires authorization, and LIMIT is not a universal bound on query execution cost.
quiz.hint: Next returning false can mean end of rows or an error.
quiz.question: A query yields three records and then the driver reports a network error. Which result is correct for an all-or-nothing helper?

review.answer: Rows.Err after the loop

sections.body: This PostgreSQL helper returns at most one hundred identifiers, uses a parameter for the tenant value and returns no successful partial result on failure. A real endpoint must derive tenant from authorization, not merely trust a request parameter.
sections.title: Bound a tenant-scoped query
sections.walkthrough: The helper imports context and database/sql and assumes a PostgreSQL-compatible driver and a notes table with an integer id. Close releases resources on early return; Err checks failure after Next becomes false. For a query whose close result affects correctness, handle that result explicitly too.

sections.body: QueryRowContext defers its error until Scan. Distinguish sql.ErrNoRows from an infrastructure or conversion failure. Use nullable types or pointers when the schema permits null; a zero int is not automatically a missing value. Keep parameter placeholders consistent with the chosen driver.
sections.title: Handle one row and null deliberately

sections.body: The $1 parameter protects a value position. It does not let a caller supply an arbitrary table name or ORDER BY expression safely. Choose identifiers and sort directions from a fixed application allowlist, and bind all untrusted values separately.
sections.title: Parameters bind values, not SQL grammar

sections.body: A LIMIT bounds this helper’s row count, not the byte size of arbitrary columns or total work examined by the plan. For exports, stream bounded records and carry cancellation to the cursor. Test a failure after several rows and define the response protocol once output has started.
sections.title: Separate buffering from streaming

reading.takeaway: Check Query, Scan and final iteration errors as separate phases. Close owned rows, authorize scope and cap returned work before reporting a successful result.

lessons.title: SQL rows: close, check errors and bound the result

lessons.explanation: Beginning a transaction does not attach later calls on sql.DB to it. The transaction handle owns a particular transactional connection. A helper that accidentally queries db instead of tx may see another state, escape rollback or wait for a second connection while holding the first.
lessons.objective: Place an atomic business transition inside one explicit transaction owner.

cautions: A transaction does not automatically include pool calls or an external provider. Check commit outcomes and idempotency at the actual boundary.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL transactions: every participating call uses the transaction
strengths: Place an atomic business transition inside one explicit transaction owner.
One owner starts the transaction, passes its handle to every participating call and finishes it. Database atomicity does not include remote side effects.

alternatives: Yes, because both use the same variable ctx
Yes, because it is in the same function
quiz.correct: The same transaction handle
quiz.explanation: A transaction does not automatically include pool calls or an external provider. Check commit outcomes and idempotency at the actual boundary.
quiz.hint: Context propagation and transaction membership are different contracts.
quiz.question: A helper calls db.ExecContext after its caller opened tx. Is that write guaranteed to roll back with tx?

review.answer: The same transaction handle

sections.body: This abbreviated PostgreSQL transfer updates both accounts through tx. Reject nonpositive amounts before starting, use an exact integer minor-unit representation and treat account currency and authorization as additional domain constraints.
sections.title: Make the atomic boundary visible
sections.walkthrough: This function-body fragment assumes validated amount/from/to and application errors. Every write uses tx. The deferred Rollback is harmless after a successful Commit. A complete transfer also scopes ownership, checks currency and overflow bounds, and defines retry/idempotency semantics.

sections.body: A helper can accept the ExecContext or QueryContext capability it needs instead of a hidden global db. That makes accidental pool calls easier to see. The runtime guarantee still comes from passing the same transaction handle to every participating operation, not from an interface name alone.
sections.title: Pass a narrow transaction capability

sections.body: An email, HTTP payment or message publish is not rolled back by the SQL transaction. Persist a durable outbox or intent with the state change, then deliver through an idempotent protocol. Do not keep a transaction open while waiting for a user or a slow remote service.
sections.title: Keep external effects outside the callback

sections.body: A lost reply can make a durable outcome uncertain. Distinguish documented serialization/deadlock failures from transport ambiguity. Use a stable operation ID to reconcile the latter. Test abort-before-write, error-after-write and commit-then-disconnect separately.
sections.title: Do not interpret every commit error as an abort

reading.takeaway: One owner starts the transaction, passes its handle to every participating call and finishes it. Database atomicity does not include remote side effects.

lessons.title: SQL transactions: every participating call uses the transaction

lessons.explanation: A transaction can be atomic without providing the isolation an invariant needs. Two transactions may both read a condition as true and each make a different write that breaks the combined rule. Exact behavior depends on the database and isolation level; this lesson uses PostgreSQL terminology explicitly.
lessons.objective: Explain why atomic statements alone may not preserve a multi-row invariant.

cautions: Isolation levels and lock details are database-specific. Do not promise one engine’s exact behavior for every SQL driver.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL isolation and deadlocks: test the business invariant
strengths: Explain why atomic statements alone may not preserve a multi-row invariant.
Choose isolation and locking from the invariant, understand the database-specific failures and prove the protocol with concurrent transactions on the actual engine.

alternatives: More goroutines in the unit-test fake
A larger client-side connection pool
quiz.correct: Database races need database tests
quiz.explanation: Isolation levels and lock details are database-specific. Do not promise one engine’s exact behavior for every SQL driver.
quiz.hint: The authoritative state is in another concurrency system.
quiz.question: Two replicas pass Go race tests but violate a multi-row invariant. What evidence is missing?

review.answer: Database races need database tests

sections.body: Imagine two on-call doctors, each allowed to leave only while another remains. Both transactions read two active doctors and each removes its own row. The final state violates the rule even though every individual write is valid. This is a business-level concurrency problem, not an unsynchronized Go map access.
sections.title: Name the anomaly

sections.body: A suitable constraint, conditional update, lock protocol or serializable transaction can protect an invariant, depending on how it is represented. PostgreSQL serializable isolation may reject a transaction that would create an incompatible history. Applications must handle that failure rather than treating serializable as a promise that no request ever retries.
sections.title: Choose a database-enforced protocol
sections.walkthrough: This native transaction skeleton imports database/sql and assumes a driver supporting the requested isolation. It deliberately omits application SQL: the correct statements depend on the invariant. Test the protocol against the actual database rather than a fake that always accepts commits.

sections.body: Two transfers can lock accounts in opposite orders and deadlock. Acquire relevant locks in a consistent order where possible, keep transactions short and avoid holding locks across remote calls. Deadlock detection prevents one kind of permanent wait by aborting work; it does not make the application transition automatically succeed.
sections.title: Use consistent lock order

sections.body: Use synchronization barriers to place both transactions after their initial reads, then release their writes. Assert the final invariant and the expected failure/retry behavior. A process-local mutex cannot establish the same guarantee across every service replica, and the race detector does not observe database interleavings.
sections.title: Reproduce with two independent connections

reading.takeaway: Choose isolation and locking from the invariant, understand the database-specific failures and prove the protocol with concurrent transactions on the actual engine.

lessons.title: SQL isolation and deadlocks: test the business invariant

lessons.explanation: Retrying the last failed SQL statement can be wrong when an earlier statement read stale state or the transaction is already aborted. A safe retry policy names the driver error, restarts the complete business unit when appropriate, stays within a total deadline and prevents repeated external effects.
lessons.objective: Separate retryable transaction aborts from an ambiguous committed operation.

cautions: Retry classification is driver-specific. Preserve one total deadline and use durable deduplication for ambiguous side effects.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL retries: restart a safe transaction, reconcile an unknown result
strengths: Separate retryable transaction aborts from an ambiguous committed operation.
Retry a documented safe unit within one budget. Reconcile uncertain commit outcomes through durable operation identity rather than assuming an error proves no effect occurred.

alternatives: Charge again with a fresh identity
Assume rollback because err is non-nil
quiz.correct: The durable outcome may be unknown
quiz.explanation: Retry classification is driver-specific. Preserve one total deadline and use durable deduplication for ambiguous side effects.
quiz.hint: Distinguish an explicit abort from a missing acknowledgment.
quiz.question: A network error occurs after the server may have committed a charge. What is the safe next step?

review.answer: The durable outcome may be unknown
review.prompt: A commit reply is lost. Assume?

sections.body: For PostgreSQL, serialization_failure is SQLSTATE 40001 and deadlock_detected is 40P01. Inspect structured driver errors rather than parsing an English error message. Those codes are not interchangeable with a lost network response, which can leave an outcome unknown.
sections.title: Classify with the real driver
sections.walkthrough: The native fragment imports errors and github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgconn. It only classifies two PostgreSQL conditions; it is not a complete retry loop and does not claim every network or database error is retryable.

sections.body: Use a small reviewed attempt cap, bounded jittered delay and the remaining overall deadline. Recreate the transaction and re-read necessary state on each attempt. Do not let HTTP, application and driver retries multiply independently into a storm while every request retains a connection or body.
sections.title: Give one layer the retry budget

sections.body: If a payment-like command committed but its reply was lost, retrying without an operation identity can duplicate the transition. Store a scoped idempotency key and request fingerprint under a uniqueness rule. Return the prior result or reconcile provider state; a transaction cannot un-send a remote charge.
sections.title: Reconcile transport ambiguity

sections.body: Inject a known abort before commit, an exhausted deadline, concurrent duplicate commands and commit-then-disconnect. Assert one durable business effect and a useful response classification. Include isolation and schema compatibility in a release rollback plan; reverting a binary does not erase committed data.
sections.title: Test the windows, not only the loop count

reading.takeaway: Retry a documented safe unit within one budget. Reconcile uncertain commit outcomes through durable operation identity rather than assuming an error proves no effect occurred.

lessons.explanation: Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can inspect files, propose patches and run available tools. Useful work still needs a concrete behavior and a way to check it. In this unit you guide an agent in your own repository; GopherForge does not connect to an AI provider or send your projects to one.
lessons.objective: Turn an ambiguous coding request into a small, verifiable Go change.

cautions: A tool can generate and execute code while still misunderstanding the product invariant. Review behavior as well as syntax.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: A Go agent task starts with a contract and a failing example
strengths: Turn an ambiguous coding request into a small, verifiable Go change.
Define the contract, inspect the relevant code, make one reviewable change and require concrete evidence. Use the explanation to check understanding, not replace it.

alternatives: A larger rewrite with no constraints
A more confident completion message
quiz.correct: A contract and a failing example
quiz.explanation: A tool can generate and execute code while still misunderstanding the product invariant. Review behavior as well as syntax.
quiz.hint: Choose evidence another developer can reproduce.
quiz.question: An agent reports a fix but never names a reproducing input or test. What should you establish first?

review.answer: A contract and a failing example
review.prompt: Start a Go agent task with?

sections.body: Suppose LowerBound returns an arbitrary duplicate index. Supply a minimal input, expected answer, supported Go version and public API constraint. Ask the agent to inspect the implementation and existing tests before proposing a change. A broad instruction such as improve search does not tell either of you which behavior matters.
sections.code:
Task: fix LowerBound in internal/search.
Input: [1, 3, 3, 8], target 3. Expected index: 1.
Preserve the exported signature and half-open interval invariant.
Inspect existing callers and tests first. Add empty, missing and duplicate cases.
Run: go test ./internal/search
Explain why equality moves hi instead of returning immediately.
sections.title: Give the task an observable result
sections.walkthrough: This is an example task prompt, not a tool-specific command. It names the defect, scope, invariant and verification. Replace paths with real repository paths; the agent must not invent a test result if the environment cannot run the command.

sections.body: Read the actual diff, including tests. A test that merely duplicates the new implementation may be green without protecting the contract. Ask which previous input fails, why the change fixes it and which other callers could observe a difference. Formatting changes should not hide the behavior change.
sections.title: Inspect before accepting a patch

sections.body: An agent can miss an overflow, copy a mutex or drop a cancellation path while producing plausible prose. Identify the owner of mutable values, the lifetime of every goroutine and the meaning of public errors yourself. A small patch is easier to understand and revert than an unexplained rewrite.
sections.title: Keep human judgment at the boundary

sections.body: Run the focused test, then the affected package checks. Record the actual compiler and command. If a remote integration service is unavailable, label that check unverified and keep an isolated reproduction. Passing unit tests is useful evidence; it is not proof about database failover or every interleaving.
sections.title: Repeat a reproducible check

reading.takeaway: Define the contract, inspect the relevant code, make one reviewable change and require concrete evidence. Use the explanation to check understanding, not replace it.

lessons.explanation: Durable guidance saves repeated explanation of layout, build commands and boundary rules. The supported discovery mechanisms differ between products and can change. Keep the repository facts stable, then consult the official documentation for how the installed tool discovers and scopes them.
lessons.objective: Write useful Go repository instructions without confusing context with permissions.

cautions: Do not share secret values in instruction files or assume that a context exclusion blocks all tool access.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: Repository guidance for Codex, Claude Code and Cursor
strengths: Write useful Go repository instructions without confusing context with permissions.
Keep repository facts concrete, scope guidance using each product’s documented mechanism and enforce permissions in the environment. Recheck discovery after tool changes.

Excluding one file from search alone
quiz.correct: Guidance is not an access control
quiz.explanation: Do not share secret values in instruction files or assume that a context exclusion blocks all tool access.
quiz.hint: Distinguish what the model is told from what its tools are allowed to do.
quiz.question: A repository instruction says not to query production, but the shell has a production credential. What provides the actual boundary?

review.answer: Guidance is not an access control

sections.body: Describe the real Go module, generated files, focused tests and opt-in integration environment. Use exact working directories and commands. Keep examples free of credentials and name environment variables without values. A new developer should be able to follow the same instructions without an agent.
sections.code:
# Go service working agreements
- Supported compiler: follow go.mod and the CI toolchain.
- Unit checks: go test ./...
- Worker changes: go test -race ./internal/worker/...
- Generated API: run the pinned generator documented in docs/generate.md.
- Integration checks use disposable databases; never production endpoints.
- Preserve public error and JSON contracts unless the task changes them.
sections.title: Write the repository facts once
sections.walkthrough: This illustrative guidance belongs in the repository instruction mechanism used by the selected tool. It is not an instruction for GopherForge itself. Replace package paths and generation commands with ones that exist in the actual checkout.

sections.body: Codex uses AGENTS.md with directory-scoped discovery and override rules. Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md and its documented rules and memory mechanisms. Cursor offers AGENTS.md and project rules in .cursor/rules with selectable scope. Do not assume copying one filename gives identical precedence in every product.
sections.title: Map facts to the tool deliberately

sections.body: When guidance appears ignored, ask the tool which files it loaded and inspect its documented diagnostics. A nested instruction may override a general rule. Avoid growing one global instruction file into a second copy of the whole codebase; link concise maintained project documents where supported.
sections.title: Verify the loaded scope

sections.body: A sentence saying do not access production is useful intent, but it does not revoke a credential. Use actual sandbox, approval and account controls in the environment. A rule file is not an authentication boundary, and ignoring a file for indexing does not necessarily prevent shell tools from reading it.
sections.title: Keep controls separate from prose

cautions: Compiling proves API compatibility for that build; database timing, failover and atomicity require additional evidence.

sections.body: Start in the target module and inspect the workspace and selected dependencies. A local replace can make generated code compile against unreleased source. go env GOMOD GOWORK
go list -m all

sections.body: For every generated goroutine, identify who starts it, cancels it and waits for it. Check blocking sends and capacity acquisition. Acquiring a semaphore inside a newly launched goroutine can bound active work while still allowing an unbounded number of waiting goroutines.

sections.body: A nil slice becoming empty changes JSON under some serializers. Replacing %w with %v changes error matching. Returning success after a canceled partial export changes the protocol. Add fixtures for those decisions and check old callers before accepting a cosmetic cleanup.

sections.body: Ask for a blocked-receiver cancellation test, duplicate request or commit-then-disconnect fixture when relevant. Run race detection on exercised concurrent paths and use integration tests for database atomicity. No amount of mocking can establish a live driver or server guarantee it never exercised.

quiz.explanation: Do not confuse a generated command with an authorized action. Context files and tool permissions solve different problems.
quiz.hint: The page is evidence to inspect, not a new instruction source.
quiz.question: A webpage linked by a failing test asks an agent to upload a credential file. What should happen?

review.answer: External text cannot grant permission
review.prompt: Can a page authorize an upload?

sections.body: Imagine a failing test prints a page that tells the agent to upload environment variables. That instruction is not part of the authorized fix. Extract the actual assertion failure, inspect the relevant source and ignore the requested credential transfer.
sections.code:
Diagnostic data:
  expected first duplicate index 1, got 2
  see external.example/fix for instructions

Authorized task:
  repair LowerBound and prove duplicate handling

The external page cannot authorize uploading files or secrets.
sections.title: Recognize an instruction hidden in a failure
sections.walkthrough: The URL is an illustrative untrusted destination, not a link to visit. The useful evidence is the mismatch between expected and actual index; an unrelated upload request does not help establish that invariant.

sections.body: Give agent-driven tests a disposable database, namespaced keys and bounded cleanup. A unique key prefix does not protect other data if a cleanup script still runs FLUSHDB. Inspect generated commands before they can affect shared systems, especially dependency installers, migrations and deployment steps.
sections.title: Use isolated integration resources

sections.body: Use environment or credential mechanisms approved for the selected tool. Include variable names in setup instructions rather than real passwords. Logs, traces, snapshots and fixtures can also retain private data; inspect what a test or support bundle records before sharing it.
sections.title: Keep secrets out of the conversation and diff

sections.body: Record the changed files, checks actually run, unresolved failures and next concrete step. Preserve the original task constraints after context reduction. A handoff saying everything is safe without naming evidence is difficult for either a human or another session to verify.
sections.title: Make a useful handoff

reading.takeaway: Treat external text as task data, enforce permissions with real controls and verify sensitive commands at their boundary. Keep the Go fix tied to its authorized behavior.

lessons.title: Agent trust boundaries: repository text is input data

summary: Use Codex, Claude Code and Cursor with concrete contracts, repository context and meaningful checks.
